power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Can affixes be recognized in a position-independent manner? A masked priming study on Tagalog prefixation and infixation
table.research_questions:
We expect to replicate the results of our previous Tagalog masked affix priming experiment where prime-target pairs sharing the same affix in the same position (tinawag-BINALIK ‘called-RETURNED’) exhibited robust priming effects. 

If morphemes that appear in different linear positions within a word are recognized in a position-independent fashion, then we predict robust priming effects for cross-position word pairs (e.g., tinali-INAKDA ‘tied-ASSIGNED’, inakda-TINALI ‘assigned-TIED’, tinali-NILASON ‘called-POISONED’, inambag-NILASON ‘contributed-POISONED’) relative to unrelated primes. This will extend Crepaldi et al.’s (2015) findings to Tagalog, showing that morphemes that can appear in different linear positions are recognized in a position-independent manner. 

Moreover, if -in- infix is easier to detect when it orthographically appears in the prefix position than the more typical infix position, as shown in the previous experiment, then we predict to find more facilitation for ni- prefixed (e.g., NILASON) and -in- infixed (e.g., TINAWAG) targets when they are preceded by -in- infix prime in the prefix position (e.g., inambag).  

Finally, if the activation of affixes happens at the abstract level, then we expect to find robust priming effects for word pairs like tinawag-NILASON ‘called-POISONED’ and inambag-NILASON ‘contributed-POISONED’, since -in- infix and ni- prefix are allomorphs of the same morpheme. 

As a control condition, if these priming effects are truly morphological, then no such facilitation should be observed for monomorphemic prime-target pairs with non-morphological orthographic overlap (e.g., lampin-LAMBAT ‘diaper-NET’).
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.

table.study_design_overview:
Design and materials

This masked affix priming experiment will be conducted in Gorilla.sc, an online experiment platform, and Tagalog speakers will be recruited as participants via Prolific. 

In this experiment, there will be four conditions, where the affixes in the prime and the target are in different orthographic linear positions: [1](a) the ʔ infix cross-position (in-INF/ʔ-INF) condition presents a target word with an -in- infix attached to a glottal stop initial stem (e.g., INUBOS from /ʔubos/ ‘consumed’) preceded by an -in- infixed word prime with the -in- following a written consonant (e.g., tinali ‘tied’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., kumuda ‘talked’) & [1](b) (ʔ-INF/in-INF) where the prime-target direction is reversed; [2](a) the  ni- prefix/-in- infix (in-INF/ni-PREF) cross-position condition presents a ni- prefixed word as a target (e.g., NIYUKO ‘bowed’) preceded by an -in- infixed word prime (e.g., binali ‘broke’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., lumagi ‘stay’) & [2](b) ʔ-INF/ni-PREF where the ni- prefixed target word is preceded by an -in- infix attached to a glottal stop initial stem (inalis-NIYUKO ‘removed-BOWED’). All unrelated primes are morphologically complex words with a different affix (i.e., -um- infix). The affixes in the related primes and unrelated primes are matched for orthographic length and linear position. There will be 40 trials in each condition.

There will also be two baseline conditions: a same position condition and an orthographic control condition, with 40 trials each. The -in- infix same position (ʔ-INF-same-pos) condition presents an -in- infixed target word attached to a glottal stop initial stem (e.g., INAYOS ‘fixed’) preceded by a prime with -in- infix appearing orthographically in the same prefix position (e.g., inusog ‘pushed’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., umandar ‘to move’). The orthographic control condition (OrthCont) consists of monomorphemic prime-target words with orthographic overlap in the first three letters (lampin-LAMBAT ‘diaper-NET’, bunyag-BUNDOL ‘reveal-HIT LIGHTLY’) and monomorphemic unrelated primes, which are words that have no orthographic overlap in the first three letters as the target (e.g., bughaw-LAMBAT ‘blue-NET’, pigtas-BUNDOL ‘break off-HIT LIGHTLY’). The overlap in the related condition is in the first three-letters, as the orthographic overlap in the critical conditions is also in that position. 

The items for the morphologically related conditions were selected by generating a large candidate set of morphologically complex words with the infix -in-, prefix ni-, and the -in- infix attached to glottal stop initial stems. As a second step, only infixed and prefixed words with 5-8 letters and with whole word frequency above 0.05 per million were retained in the candidate sets. Target words were pairwise matched with related and unrelated primes for orthographic length. To generate unrelated prime words, we generated a large candidate set of -um- infixed words that are 5-8 letters long with a lexical frequency of above 0.05 per million. Unrelated primes were pairwise matched with related primes for orthographic length and whole word lexical frequency. Due to limited items, the related primes in the in-INF/ʔ-INF condition were repeated as targets in the ʔ-INF/in-INF condition. Moreover, the related primes in the ʔ-IN/ni-PREF condition were repeated as targets in the ʔ-INF-same-pos condition. Some unrelated primes in the ʔ-INF/ni-PREF condition were also repeated as unrelated primes in the ʔ-INF-same-pos condition. To reduce long-lag priming, these repeated items were separated into different blocks, making a total of 4 blocks in this experiment.

To generate items for the orthographic control condition, the first author, who is a native Tagalog speaker, created word pairs with first three-letter overlap (e.g., lampin-LAMBAT ‘diaper-NET’, bunyag-BUNDOL ‘reveal-HIT LIGHTLY’). Monomorphemic words were assigned as an unrelated prime if they had no orthographic overlap in the first three letters with the target word. Only words that are 4-8 letters long with a lexical frequency above 0.05 per million were retained from the candidate set. As a second step, Levenshtein distance (Levenshtein, 1965) was used to derive an orthographic overlap score. Only word pairs with a Levenshtein score of <4 were included in the related condition, while word pairs with a Levenshtein score of >5 were included in the unrelated condition.

Lexical frequencies were obtained from SketchEngine, an online platform that compiles web-based text corpora from more than 900 languages. The most recent version of the Tagalog corpus in this platform has 198, 303, 250 words. The targets in the ʔ-INF/in-INF, in-INF/ʔ-INF, ni-PREF/ʔ-INF, ni-PREF/ʔ-INF, in-INF-same-pos, and OrthCont conditions were list-wise matched as close as possible for orthographic length and lexical frequency. Further, the related and unrelated primes were pairwise and list-wise matched as close as possible for lexical frequency and orthographic length. The same matching were employed in the OrthCont condition. All targets and primes in the final stimulus list are words with frequencies above 0.05 per million in SketchEngine. Since primes and targets both range in length between 4-8 characters, a forward mask of 8 #s were chosen to ensure complete masking of all primes, and that no cue to prime or target length is provided by the mask. A proportional font, in which each character takes up the same amount of space, were used to ensure the forward mask completely covers the same visual range as the prime, and that the prime and target extend over the same visual range. 

A set of nonword primes and targets were generated using the pseudoword generator toolkit Wuggy by scrambling possible syllables using real Tagalog words as training input (Keuleers & Brysbaert, 2010). In Wuggy, the real word training inputs and the nonword outputs were matched in length of subsyllabic segments, letter length, and transition frequencies (i.e., the number of words in which two specific subsyllabic elements occur in sequence). A total of 240 nonword targets and 120 nonwords primes were selected in the final stimulus list to serve as filler trials. All nonword primes and targets that were selected are pronounceable nonwords ranging between 4-8 characters to match the critical and control trials. The other half of the nonword targets were preceded by real word primes to avoid cueing participants to the lexical decision they should make. The real word primes are 6-8 characters long. Both nonword and real word primes were list-wise and pairwise matched for orthographic length. Moreover, both real word and nonword primes were pairwise matched to the targets for orthographic length to match the critical and control conditions.

This resulted in a total of 240 trials (120 related and 120 unrelated) in this experiment, which were pseudo-interleaved with 240 filler trials, consisting of 120 nonword-nonword (NW-NW) prime-target pairs (e.g., dukmo-BABAG) and 120 word-nonword (W-NW) pairs (e.g., hiling-BALTAY 'request'-BALTAY). We created 10 practice trials. Overall, the entire experiment consists of 490 trials. 

The masked prime will be presented for 33ms, following previous masked affix priming experiments. The primes will be masked by being preceded by strings of number signs (e.g., ########) for 500ms. The forward mask will be preceded by a fixation cross for 500ms. Native Tagalog speakers will have 2500ms to judge whether the target word is a real Tagalog word or not by pressing the corresponding arrow key. If no response is registered, the experiment will automatically proceed to the next trial. Participants will be continuously cued by TUNAY ‘Yes’ and HINDI ‘No’ on opposite sides of the screen. For half of the participants, TUNAY maps to the left arrow key and HINDI maps to the right arrow key, while the other half will apply the opposite mappings. Overall, a complete trial sequence is as follows: [+ for 500ms] [######## for 500ms] [prime for 33ms] [TARGET for 2500ms or until button press] [ISI 1000ms]. Targets will be presented in upper case, and primes in lower case - the case change is necessary to create a visual change between the prime and target in the critical condition.  

The experiment is a within-subject design - all participants will see the critical targets in both their related prime and unrelated prime condition. The two occurrences of each target will be separated in different blocks, with a short break in between. The order of items within a block will be pseudo-randomised for each participant, and the order of the four blocks will be permuted across participants such that each block occurs as the first block for ¼ of participants. Participants will be randomly assigned to each experimental list. 

Procedure

The experiment consists of a lexical decision task in which participants are presented with strings of letters appearing in the middle of the screen, and their task is to say whether a string is an existing word of their native language. To give their answers, the participants are instructed to use the arrows on the keyboard. For half of the participants, the left arrow corresponds to “yes”, and the right one to “no”, while the other half of the participants receives the opposite instructions. 

The task is preceded by a consent form at the beginning of the experiment. After the consent form, the instructions appear on the screen, followed by 10 practice trials. Feedback is provided during the practice trials. The participants are then notified that the practice is over, and that feedback will not be provided from then on, after which they can start the experiment. The main experiment contains 480 trials divided into 4 blocks with 120 trials each. A break is given after each block. At the beginning of each trial, a fixation cross appears for 500 ms, followed by the stimulus that stays on the screen for 2.5 seconds or until the participant answers. A blank screen between the stimuli is also added with the duration of 1000 ms. After the last trial, a short debriefing is presented, describing the aims of the experiment, and offering the opportunity to leave comments. The last part of the experiment is a language questionnaire. The questionnaire includes questions about the participants’ native language(s), country of birth and schooling, and other questions that might be relevant for understanding the participant language profile (see below in Other).
table.randomization: Each participant will randomly be assigned to a list in which the “yes” answer is on the left, or a version where “yes” is on the right side¬, using Balanced Randomization mode to an ensure equal number of participants per version. Moreover, trials at each run will be randomized using the randomise_trials column in the Gorilla spreadsheet, so that the order of the item presentation is different for each participant.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: The recruitment will be done via Prolific (https://www.prolific.co/). We will screen participants for age (over 18), native/first language (Tagalog), city where they originated from in the Philippines, and device (desktop or laptop, but not tablet or mobile). Participants will be directed to the study on Gorilla. At the end of the experiment, they will be directed back to Prolific. Participants will be remunerated the equivalent of £7.50/hr for their participation via the Prolific platform (the experiment takes between 20 and 30 minutes).
table.sample_size: An initial sample of 70 participants will be recruited in this experiment. We will then determine which proportion of primes for each participant was recorded by Gorilla as being presented for the target duration (33ms), and which proportion were recorded as presented for longer. Primes presented for longer than 60ms (the upper limit for masked priming effects reported in the literature) will be flagged. If 10% or more of primes for a participant exceed 60ms, that participant will be excluded from analysis and additional participants will be recruited until we have 70 participants with 90% prime duration accuracy and 80% accuracy on the critical trials. A complete analysis of the data will then be undertaken.
table.sample_size_rationale: We will be recruiting 70 native Tagalog speakers. The sample size is designed to follow the previous masked affix priming experiment we conducted in Gorilla, where we successfully replicated robust priming effects for prime-target pairs that share the same affix, while no such effects were found for prime-target pairs that share non-morphological orthographic overlap.
table.stopping_rule: If the target results are not replicated with 70 participants (see Hypothesis section), the study will be terminated.
table.manipulated_variables: The variables that are manipulated for the experiment are Relation Type and Prime Type. The Relation Type variable controls the types of morphological relationship between the prime and the target, which can either be morphologically related (in-INF/ʔ-INF, ʔ-INF/in-INF, ʔ-INF/ni-PREF, in-INF/ni-PREF, in-INF-same-pos) or orthographically related (OrthCont). The Prime Type variable controls the relatedness between the prime and the target, which can be related (morphologically and orthographically) or completely unrelated.
table.measured_variables: Participants’ Reaction Time (RT) to targets when preceded by the related and unrelated primes will be compared in this study (see Analysis Plan). Participants’ lexical decision accuracy on each trial will determine whether that trial is included or excluded, and participant accuracy rates will determine whether a participant is included or excluded (see Exclusion Criteria).
table.statistical_tests:
We will use Mixed-Effects regression analyses in the lme4 package in R. The model will have Reaction Time (RT) as the dependent variable and RelationType (in-INF/ʔ-INF, ʔ-INF/in-INF, ʔ-INF/ni-PREF, in-INF/ni-PREF, in-INF-same-pos, and OrthCont) crossed with PrimeType (related, unrelated) as fixed effects. The baseline level for PrimeType will be ‘Unrelated’. For RelationType, the baseline will first be ʔ-INF/in-INF to allow comparison with the reversed condition in-INF/ʔ-INF. We will then set the baseline to ni-PREF/ʔ-INF to allow comparison with ni-PREF/in-INF. By-subject and by-item random slopes and intercepts will be included as random effects. The initial full model will be coded as: TagPrime ← lmer(RT ~ RelationType * PrimeType + (RelationType*PrimeType|Subject) + (RelationType*PrimeType|Item), REML = F). To choose the best random effects structure, Log-likelihood ratio testing will be used. We will compare models with by-subject and by-item random slopes to the model with only a by-subject random slope. If the less complicated model is more parsimonious based on BIC and AIC, then we will simplify the model by dropping the random slope for items. The same process will be applied to by-subject random slope. 

The full model with RelationType * PrimeType interaction will be compared to the model without interaction RelationType + PrimeType. If the less complex model has better goodness of fit, the model will be further simplified by removing RelationType as a factor and compared to the model with this factor. Since the critical criterion for assessing whether we get masked priming effects is obtaining significant priming in the ʔ-INF/in-INF, in-INF/ʔ-INF, ni-PREF/ʔ-INF, ni-PREF/in-INF, in-INF-same-pos, but no significant OrthCont priming, the RelationType is the most important factor. If RelationType does not make a significant contribution to the model’s goodness of fit, we will consider that we have failed to find the effect.

Multiple comparison corrections will be done using the emmeans package in R, particularly Tukey HSD, which will be coded as: TagPrime.emm = emmans(TagPrime, ~ RelationType * PrimeType), then pairs(TagPrime.emm, simple = “each”). This will generate simple main-effect contrast sets, comparing the magnitude of RelationType * PrimeType interaction effects across conditions.
table.inference_criteria: We will be using the T value >|2| criteria to evaluate significance in our linear mixed models. We are also expecting an effect size of > 20ms for the in-INF/ʔ-INF, ʔ-INF/in-INF, ʔ-INF/ni-PREF, in-INF/ni-PREF, and in-INF-same-pos priming effect, which is the effect size commonly reported in masked affix priming literature (see Crepaldi et al., 2015).
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Prior to data analysis, participant error rates for the grammatical items will be calculated. Participants rejecting more than 20% of the grammatical items will be excluded from analysis. Participants who don’t list Tagalog as of their native language, and who attended primary and secondary school outside of the Philippines will be removed.

Only accurate response data will be included in the RT analyses. We will first remove responses shorter than 200 ms. Further outlier removal will be performed following Baayen and Millin (2010), by fitting a simple mixed model with only random effects and excluding all data points with residuals exceeding 2.5 SD.
table.missing_data_handling: The lmer function in R removes the missing data.

table.title: Does affix linear position matter during morpheme detection process? Evidence from a Tagalog masked affix priming experiment
table.research_questions:
If affixes are actively processed during morphological processing and are represented in the human mind, then we expect to find robust priming effects for -in- INF, -um- INF, ni- PREF, and ʔ-INF conditions, where the prime-target pairs share the same affix. These findings would be consistent with previous masked affix priming studies in English (Chateau et al., 2002, Crepaldi et al., 2015, Duñabeitia et al., 2008), French (Giraudo & Grainger, 2003), Spanish (Dominguez et al., 2010), Maltese (Ussishkin et al., 2015), and Arabic (Boudelaa & Marslen-Wilson, 2005).

Moreover, if these priming effects are truly morphological, then no such facilitation should be observed for monomorphemic prime-target pairs with non-morphological orthographic overlap (e.g., lampin-LAMBAT ‘diaper-NET’). 

If affix linear position affects morphological detection process, then we predict to find less robust priming effects for -in- INF and -um- INF conditions than ni-PREF and potentially ʔ-INF conditions. This would be consistent with models like “beginning-to-end” sequential bias (see Diependaele et al., 2009). Importantly, ʔ-INF condition may behave like a prefix since it is orthographically left-edge aligned or like an infix due to being phonologically non-edge aligned. Tagalog allows us to tease these possibilities apart.

Finally, if a viable stem is required to trigger form-based decomposition mechanisms (see Gwilliams & Marantz, 2018), then no priming effects should be obtained for -in- Pseudo-INF and -um- Pseudo-INF conditions. This would contract the previous Tagalog neuroimaging study of Wray et al. (2022).
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
table.study_design_overview:
This masked affix priming experiment will be conducted in Gorilla.sc, an online experiment platform, and Tagalog speakers will be recruited as participants via Prolific. 

This experiment will have four conditions containing real affixed words, with 40 trials each: [1] -in- INF condition presents an -in- infixed target word (e.g., TINUMBA ‘got knocked down’) that can be preceded by another -in- infixed prime (e.g., binalik ‘returned’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., bumalik ‘returned’); [2] -um- INF condition presents an -um- infixed target word (e.g., SUMABOG ‘to explode’) that can be preceded by another -um- infixed prime (e.g., tumapak ‘to step’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., tinaboy ‘to repell’); [3] ni- PREF condition presents a ni-prefixed target word (e.g., NILASON ‘poisoned’) that can be preceded by another ni-prefixed prime (e.g., ninakaw ‘stole’) or an unrelated prime (e.g.,  umatras ‘retreated’); and [4] ʔ-INF condition presents a target word with an -in- infix attached to a glottal initial stem (e.g., INUBOS ‘consumed’) that can be preceded by a prime with the same affix (e.g., inayos ‘fixed’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., umayos ‘fixed’). Unrelated primes are morphologically complex words with a different affix as the target word (i.e., -in- for -um- INF condition and -um- for all other conditions). The affixes in the related primes and unrelated primes are matched for orthographic length and linear position.

The items for -in- INF, -um- INF, ni- PREF, and ʔ-INF conditions will be selected by generating a large candidate set of morphologically complex words with the infixes -in-, -um-, and the prefix ni-. As a second step, only infixed and prefixed words with 5-8 letters and with whole word frequency above 0.05 per million will be retained in the candidate sets. Target words will be pairwise matched with related and unrelated primes for orthographic length. Unrelated primes will be pairwise matched with related primes for orthographic length and lexical frequency.

There will be two conditions containing pseudo-infixed words, with 32 trials each: [1] -in- Pseudo-INF condition presents a monomorphemic target word with -in- orthographic unit in the first syllable (e.g., KINTAB ‘shine’), which can be preceded by another pseudo-infixed prime (e.g., mintis ‘failure’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., suwero ‘serum’); and [2] -um- Pseudo-INF condition presents a monomorphemic target word with -um- orthographic unit in the first syllable (e.g., TUMPOK ‘pile’) that can be preceded by another pseudo-infixed prime (e.g., lumpia ‘spring rolls’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., tigbak ‘bump’). Unrelated primes are monomorphemic words with no -in- and -um- orthographic unit in the first syllable.

Crucially, there will be an orthographic control (Orth.Con) condition with 40 trials. This orthographic control condition will consist of monomorphemic prime-target words with orthographic overlap in the first three letters (lampin-LAMBAT ‘diaper-NET’, bunyag-BUNDOL ‘reveal-HIT LIGHTLY’). These monomorphemic target words can also be preceded by unrelated primes, which are words that have no overlap in the first three letters as the target (e.g., bughaw-LAMBAT ‘blue-NET’, pigtas-BUNDOL ‘break off-HIT LIGHTLY’). We decided to have first three-letter overlap in this condition, as the orthographic overlap in the critical conditions are also in that position. 

The first author, who is a native Tagalog speaker, will create word pairs with first three-letter overlap (e.g., lampin-LAMBAT ‘diaper-NET’, bunyag-BUNDOL ‘reveal-HIT LIGHTLY’). Monomorphemic words will be assigned as unrelated primes if they have no orthographic overlap in the first three letters as the target words. Only words that are 4-8 letter long with lexical frequency of above 0.05 per million will be retained from the candidate set. As a second step, Levenshtein distance (Levenshtein, 1965) will be used to derive an orthographic overlap score. Only word pairs with a Levenshtein score of <4 will be included in the related condition, while word pairs with a Levenshtein score of >5 will be included in the unrelated condition.

There will be a total of 264 critical trials (132 related and 132 unrelated) in this experiment, which will be pseudo-interleaved with 264 filler trials, consisting of 132 nonword-nonword (NW-NW) prime-target pairs (e.g., dukmo-BABAG) and 132 word-nonword (W-NW) pairs (e.g., hiling-BALTAY 'request'-BALTAY). There will be 10 practice trials. Overall, the entire experiment will consist of 538 trials. 

Lexical frequencies will be obtained from SketchEngine, an online platform that compiles web-based text corpora from more than 900 languages. The most recent version of the Tagalog corpus in this platform has 198, 303, 250 words. The targets in the -in- INF, -um- INF, ni- PREF, and ʔ-INF conditions will be list-wise matched as close as possible for orthographic length and lexical frequency. Further, the target, related, and unrelated primes will be pairwise matched for orthographic length. Related and unrelated primes will be pairwise and list-wise matched as close as possible for lexical frequency. The same matching will be employed in the Orth.Con condition. All targets and primes in the final stimulus list will be words with frequencies above 0.05 per million. Since primes and targets both range in length between 4-8 characters, a forward mask of 8 #s will be chosen to ensure complete masking of all primes, and that no cue to prime or target length is provided by the mask. A proportional font, in which each character takes up the same amount of space, will be used to ensure the forward mask completely covers the same visual range as the prime, and that the prime and target extend over the same visual range. 

A set of nonword primes and targets will be generated using the pseudoword generator toolkit Wuggy by scrambling possible syllables using real Tagalog words as training input (Keuleers & Brysbaert, 2010). In Wuggy, the real word training inputs and the nonword outputs will be matched in length of subsyllabic segments, letter length, and transition frequencies (i.e., the number of words in which two specific subsyllabic elements occur in sequence). A total of 264 nonword targets and 132 nonwords primes will be selected in the final stimulus list to serve as filler trials. All nonword primes and targets that will be selected are pronounceable nonwords ranging between 4-8 characters to match the critical and control trials. The other half of the nonword targets will be preceded by real word primes to avoid cueing participants to the lexical decision they should make. The real word primes are 4-8 characters long. Both nonword and real word primes will be list-wise matched for orthographic length. Moreover, both real word and nonword primes will be pairwise matched with their nonword target for orthographic length to match the critical and control conditions.

The masked prime will be presented for 33ms. The primes will be masked by being preceded by strings of number signs (e.g., ########) for 500ms. The forward mask will be preceded by a fixation cross for 500ms. Native Tagalog speakers will have 2500ms to judge whether the target word is a real Tagalog word or not by pressing the corresponding arrow key. If no response is registered, the experiment will automatically proceed to the next trial. Participants will be continuously cued by TUNAY ‘Yes’ and HINDI ‘No’ on opposite sides of the screen. For half of the participants, TUNAY maps to the left arrow key and HINDI maps to the right arrow key, while the other half will apply the opposite mappings. Overall, a complete trial sequence is as follows: [+ for 500ms] [######## for 500ms] [prime for 33ms] [TARGET for 2500ms or until button press] [ISI 1000ms]. Targets will be presented in upper case, and primes in lower case - the case change is necessary to create a visual change between the prime and target in the critical condition.  

The experiment is a within-subject design - all participants will see the critical targets in both their related prime and unrelated prime conditions. The two occurrences of each target will be separated into two separate blocks, with a short break in between. The order of items within a block will be pseudo-randomised for each participant, and the order of the two blocks will be permuted across participants such that each block occurs as the first block for 1/2 of participants and as the second block for the other half. 

Procedure

The experiment consists of a lexical decision task in which participants are presented with strings of letters appearing in the middle of the screen, and their task is to say whether a string is an existing word of their native language. To give their answers, the participants are instructed to use the arrows on the keyboard. For half of the participants, the left arrow corresponds to “yes”, and the right one to “no”, while the other half of the participants receives the opposite instructions. 

The task is preceded by a consent form at the beginning of the experiment. After the consent form, the instructions appear on the screen, followed by 10 practice trials. Feedback is provided during the practice trials. The participants are then notified that the practice is over, and that feedback will not be provided from then on, after which they can start the experiment. The main experiment contains 528 trials, with a break half-way through after 264 trials. At the beginning of each trial, a fixation cross appears for 500 ms, followed by the stimulus that stays on the screen for 2.5 seconds or until the participant answers. A blank screen between the stimuli is also added with the duration of 1000ms. After the last trial, a short debriefing is presented, describing the aims of the experiment, and offering the opportunity to leave comments. The last part of the experiment is a language questionnaire. The questionnaire includes questions about the participants’ native language(s), country of birth and schooling, and other questions that might be relevant for understanding the participant language profile (see below in Other).
table.randomization: Each participant will randomly be assigned to a list in which the “yes” answer is on the left, or a version where “yes” is on the right side¬, using Balanced Randomization mode to an ensure equal number of participants per version. Moreover, trials at each run will be randomized using the randomise_trials column in the Gorilla spreadsheet, so that the order of the item presentation is different for each participant.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: The recruitment will be done via Prolific (https://www.prolific.co/). We will screen participants for age (over 18), native/first language (Tagalog), city where they originated from the Philippines, and device (desktop or laptop, but not tablet or mobile). Participants will be directed to the study on Gorilla. At the end of the experiment, they will be directed back to Prolific. Participants will be renumerated the equivalent of £7.50/hr for their participation via the Prolific platform (the experiment takes between 20 and 30 minutes).
table.sample_size: Data collection will be done using sequential samples. An initial sample of 40 participants will be recruited. We will then determine which proportion of primes for each participant was recorded by Gorilla as being presented for the intended duration (33ms), and which proportion were recorded as presented for longer. Primes presented for longer than 60ms (the upper limit for masked priming effects reported in the literature) will be flagged. If 10% or more of primes for a participant exceed 60ms, that participant will be excluded from analysis and additional participants will be recruited until we have 40 participants with 90% prime duration accuracy. A complete analysis of the data will then be undertaken. Another set of 40 participants will be recruited and the data will go through the same pre-processing stages and analyses.
table.sample_size_rationale: The initial sample size is designed to follow the previous masked priming experiment we conducted in Gorilla, where we successfully replicated masked morphological priming effects with 80 participants. However, it has to be noted that the current experiment has a more fine-grained morphological relatedness (only sharing an affix), rather than a simple stem overlap. The sequential sampling plan, up to a maximum of 120 participants, is motivated both by research comparing Internet-based data to lab-based data, which has shown that the data quality is similar as long as the Internet-based sample size is at least three times larger than the lab-based sample size (Gosling et al., 2004). The number of participants in the lab-based experiments employing lexical decision task from the previous studies varies between 20 and 46 (Manouilidou, 2007; Manouilidou & Stockall, 2014, Neophytou et al 2018, Stockall et al 2019), so we considered 80-120 to be an appropriate number for an online masked affix priming experiment.
table.stopping_rule: Depending on the findings, we will either stop or run one more set of 40 participants, then analyze their RT again, again excluding and replacing participants with >10% prime duration error. If the target results are not replicated with 120 participants (see Hypothesis section), the study will be terminated.
table.manipulated_variables:
The variables that are manipulated for the experiment are Relation Type and Prime Type. The Relation Type variable controls the types of relationship between the prime and the target, which can either be truly morphologically related (e.g., -in- INF, -um- INF, ni- PREF, and ʔ-INF), pseudo morphologically related (-in- Pseudo-INF, -um- Pseudo-INF), or orthographically related (Orth.Con). The Prime Type variable controls the relatedness between the prime and the target, which can be related (morphologically, pseudo-morphologically, or orthographically) or completely unrelated. 

We also added filler items, which do not form part of the main analysis.
table.measured_variables: Participants’ Reaction Time (RT) to the target when preceded by related and unrelated primes will be compared in this study (see Analysis Plan). Participants’ lexical decision accuracy on each trial will determine whether that trial is included or excluded, and participant accuracy rates will determine whether a participant is included or excluded (see Exclusion Criteria).
table.statistical_tests:
We will use Mixed-Effects regression analyses in the lme4 package in R. The model will have Reaction Time (RT) as the dependent variable and RelationType (-in- INF, -um- INF, ni- PREF, ʔ-INF, -in- Pseudo-INF, -um- Pseudo-INF, Orth.Con) crossed with PrimeType (related, unrelated) as fixed effects. The baseline levels for the two fixed factors will be ‘-in- INF’ and ‘unrelated’, respectively. By-subject and by-item random slopes and intercepts will be included as random effects. The initial full model will be coded as: TagPrime ← lmer(RT ~ RelationType * PrimeType + (RelationType*PrimeType|Subject) + (RelationType*PrimeType|Item), REML = F). To choose the best random effects structure, Log-likelihood ratio testing will be used. We will compare models with by-subject and by-item random slopes to the model with only a by-subject random slope. If the less complicated model is more parsimonious based on BIC and AIC, then we will simplify the model by dropping the random slope for items. The same process will be applied to by-subject random slope. 

The full model with RelationType * PrimeType interaction will be compared to the model without interaction RelationType + PrimeType. If the less complex model has better goodness of fit, the model will be further simplified by removing RelationType as a factor and compared to the model with this factor. Since the critical criterion for assessing whether we get masked priming effects is obtaining significant priming in -in- INF, -um- INF, ni- PREF, and ʔ-INF (potentially -in- Pseudo-INF, -um- Pseudo-INF), but no significant Orth.Con priming, the RelationType is the most important factor. If RelationType does not make a significant contribution to the model’s goodness of fit, we will consider that we have failed to find the effect.

We will also run separate analyses where the -in- Pseudo-INF and -um- Pseudo-INF conditions will be collapsed into one condition Pseudo-INF to further investigate the decomposition of pseudo-infixed words. 

Multiple comparison corrections will be done using the emmeans package in R, particularly Tukey HSD, which will be coded as: TagPrime.emm = emmans(TagPrime, ~ RelationType * PrimeType), then pairs(TagPrime.emm, simple = “each”). This will generate simple main-effect contrast sets, comparing the magnitude of RelationType * PrimeType interaction effects across conditions.
table.inference_criteria: We will be using the T value >|2| criteria to evaluate significance in our linear mixed models. We are also expecting an effect size of > 20ms for the -in- INF, -um- INF, ni PREF, and ʔ-INF priming effect, which is the effect size commonly reported in masked affix priming literature (see Crepaldi et al., 2015).
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Prior to data analysis, participant error rates for the grammatical items will be calculated. Participants rejecting more than 20% of the real word items will be excluded from analysis. Participants who don’t list Tagalog as of their native language, and who attended primary and secondary school outside of the Philippines will be removed.

Only accurate response data will be included in the RT analyses. We will first remove responses shorter than 200 ms. Further outlier removal will be performed following Baayen and Millin (2010), by fitting a simple mixed model with only random effects and excluding all data points with residuals exceeding 2.5 SD.

table.title: Can affixes be recognized in a position-independent manner? A masked priming study on Tagalog prefixation and infixation
table.research_questions:
We expect to replicate the results of our previous Tagalog masked affix priming experiment where prime-target pairs sharing the same affix in the same position (tinawag-BINALIK ‘called-RETURNED’) exhibited robust priming effects. 

If morphemes that appear in different linear positions within a word are recognized in a position-independent fashion, then we predict robust priming effects for cross-position word pairs (e.g., tinali-INAKDA ‘tied-ASSIGNED’, inakda-TINALI ‘assigned-TIED’, tinali-NILASON ‘called-POISONED’, inambag-NILASON ‘contributed-POISONED’) relative to unrelated primes. This will extend Crepaldi et al.’s (2015) findings to Tagalog, showing that morphemes that can appear in different linear positions are recognized in a position-independent manner. 

Moreover, if -in- infix is easier to detect when it orthographically appears in the prefix position than the more typical infix position, as shown in the previous experiment, then we predict to find more facilitation for ni- prefixed (e.g., NILASON) and -in- infixed (e.g., TINAWAG) targets when they are preceded by -in- infix prime in the prefix position (e.g., inambag).  

Finally, if the activation of affixes happens at the abstract level, then we expect to find robust priming effects for word pairs like tinawag-NILASON ‘called-POISONED’ and inambag-NILASON ‘contributed-POISONED’, since -in- infix and ni- prefix are allomorphs of the same morpheme. 

As a control condition, if these priming effects are truly morphological, then no such facilitation should be observed for monomorphemic prime-target pairs with non-morphological orthographic overlap (e.g., lampin-LAMBAT ‘diaper-NET’).

table.study_design_overview:
Design and materials

This masked affix priming experiment will be conducted in Gorilla.sc, an online experiment platform, and Tagalog speakers will be recruited as participants via Prolific. 

In this experiment, there will be four conditions, where the affixes in the prime and the target are in different orthographic linear positions: [1](a) the ʔ infix cross-position (in-INF/ʔ-INF) condition presents a target word with an -in- infix attached to a glottal stop initial stem (e.g., INUBOS from /ʔubos/ ‘consumed’) preceded by an -in- infixed word prime with the -in- following a written consonant (e.g., tinali ‘tied’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., kumuda ‘talked’) & [1](b) (ʔ-INF/in-INF) where the prime-target direction is reversed; [2](a) the  ni- prefix/-in- infix (in-INF/ni-PREF) cross-position condition presents a ni- prefixed word as a target (e.g., NIYUKO ‘bowed’) preceded by an -in- infixed word prime (e.g., binali ‘broke’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., lumagi ‘stay’) & [2](b) ʔ-INF/ni-PREF where the ni- prefixed target word is preceded by an -in- infix attached to a glottal stop initial stem (inalis-NIYUKO ‘removed-BOWED’). All unrelated primes are morphologically complex words with a different affix (i.e., -um- infix). The affixes in the related primes and unrelated primes are matched for orthographic length and linear position. There will be 40 trials in each condition.

There will also be two baseline conditions: a same position condition and an orthographic control condition, with 40 trials each. The -in- infix same position (ʔ-INF-same-pos) condition presents an -in- infixed target word attached to a glottal stop initial stem (e.g., INAYOS ‘fixed’) preceded by a prime with -in- infix appearing orthographically in the same prefix position (e.g., inusog ‘pushed’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., umandar ‘to move’). The orthographic control condition (OrthCont) consists of monomorphemic prime-target words with orthographic overlap in the first three letters (lampin-LAMBAT ‘diaper-NET’, bunyag-BUNDOL ‘reveal-HIT LIGHTLY’) and monomorphemic unrelated primes, which are words that have no orthographic overlap in the first three letters as the target (e.g., bughaw-LAMBAT ‘blue-NET’, pigtas-BUNDOL ‘break off-HIT LIGHTLY’). The overlap in the related condition is in the first three-letters, as the orthographic overlap in the critical conditions is also in that position. 

The items for the morphologically related conditions were selected by generating a large candidate set of morphologically complex words with the infix -in-, prefix ni-, and the -in- infix attached to glottal stop initial stems. As a second step, only infixed and prefixed words with 5-8 letters and with whole word frequency above 0.05 per million were retained in the candidate sets. Target words were pairwise matched with related and unrelated primes for orthographic length. To generate unrelated prime words, we generated a large candidate set of -um- infixed words that are 5-8 letters long with a lexical frequency of above 0.05 per million. Unrelated primes were pairwise matched with related primes for orthographic length and whole word lexical frequency. Due to limited items, the related primes in the in-INF/ʔ-INF condition were repeated as targets in the ʔ-INF/in-INF condition. Moreover, the related primes in the ʔ-IN/ni-PREF condition were repeated as targets in the ʔ-INF-same-pos condition. Some unrelated primes in the ʔ-INF/ni-PREF condition were also repeated as unrelated primes in the ʔ-INF-same-pos condition. To reduce long-lag priming, these repeated items were separated into different blocks, making a total of 4 blocks in this experiment.

To generate items for the orthographic control condition, the first author, who is a native Tagalog speaker, created word pairs with first three-letter overlap (e.g., lampin-LAMBAT ‘diaper-NET’, bunyag-BUNDOL ‘reveal-HIT LIGHTLY’). Monomorphemic words were assigned as an unrelated prime if they had no orthographic overlap in the first three letters with the target word. Only words that are 4-8 letters long with a lexical frequency above 0.05 per million were retained from the candidate set. As a second step, Levenshtein distance (Levenshtein, 1965) was used to derive an orthographic overlap score. Only word pairs with a Levenshtein score of <4 were included in the related condition, while word pairs with a Levenshtein score of >5 were included in the unrelated condition.

Lexical frequencies were obtained from SketchEngine, an online platform that compiles web-based text corpora from more than 900 languages. The most recent version of the Tagalog corpus in this platform has 198, 303, 250 words. The targets in the ʔ-INF/in-INF, in-INF/ʔ-INF, ni-PREF/ʔ-INF, ni-PREF/ʔ-INF, in-INF-same-pos, and OrthCont conditions were list-wise matched as close as possible for orthographic length and lexical frequency. Further, the related and unrelated primes were pairwise and list-wise matched as close as possible for lexical frequency and orthographic length. The same matching were employed in the OrthCont condition. All targets and primes in the final stimulus list are words with frequencies above 0.05 per million in SketchEngine. Since primes and targets both range in length between 4-8 characters, a forward mask of 8 #s were chosen to ensure complete masking of all primes, and that no cue to prime or target length is provided by the mask. A proportional font, in which each character takes up the same amount of space, were used to ensure the forward mask completely covers the same visual range as the prime, and that the prime and target extend over the same visual range. 

A set of nonword primes and targets were generated using the pseudoword generator toolkit Wuggy by scrambling possible syllables using real Tagalog words as training input (Keuleers & Brysbaert, 2010). In Wuggy, the real word training inputs and the nonword outputs were matched in length of subsyllabic segments, letter length, and transition frequencies (i.e., the number of words in which two specific subsyllabic elements occur in sequence). A total of 240 nonword targets and 120 nonwords primes were selected in the final stimulus list to serve as filler trials. All nonword primes and targets that were selected are pronounceable nonwords ranging between 4-8 characters to match the critical and control trials. The other half of the nonword targets were preceded by real word primes to avoid cueing participants to the lexical decision they should make. The real word primes are 6-8 characters long. Both nonword and real word primes were list-wise and pairwise matched for orthographic length. Moreover, both real word and nonword primes were pairwise matched to the targets for orthographic length to match the critical and control conditions.

This resulted in a total of 240 trials (120 related and 120 unrelated) in this experiment, which were pseudo-interleaved with 240 filler trials, consisting of 120 nonword-nonword (NW-NW) prime-target pairs (e.g., dukmo-BABAG) and 120 word-nonword (W-NW) pairs (e.g., hiling-BALTAY 'request'-BALTAY). We created 10 practice trials. Overall, the entire experiment consists of 490 trials. 

The masked prime will be presented for 33ms, following previous masked affix priming experiments. The primes will be masked by being preceded by strings of number signs (e.g., ########) for 500ms. The forward mask will be preceded by a fixation cross for 500ms. Native Tagalog speakers will have 2500ms to judge whether the target word is a real Tagalog word or not by pressing the corresponding arrow key. If no response is registered, the experiment will automatically proceed to the next trial. Participants will be continuously cued by TUNAY ‘Yes’ and HINDI ‘No’ on opposite sides of the screen. For half of the participants, TUNAY maps to the left arrow key and HINDI maps to the right arrow key, while the other half will apply the opposite mappings. Overall, a complete trial sequence is as follows: [+ for 500ms] [######## for 500ms] [prime for 33ms] [TARGET for 2500ms or until button press] [ISI 1000ms]. Targets will be presented in upper case, and primes in lower case - the case change is necessary to create a visual change between the prime and target in the critical condition.  

The experiment is a within-subject design - all participants will see the critical targets in both their related prime and unrelated prime condition. The two occurrences of each target will be separated in different blocks, with a short break in between. The order of items within a block will be pseudo-randomised for each participant, and the order of the four blocks will be permuted across participants such that each block occurs as the first block for ¼ of participants. Participants will be randomly assigned to each experimental list. 

Procedure

The experiment consists of a lexical decision task in which participants are presented with strings of letters appearing in the middle of the screen, and their task is to say whether a string is an existing word of their native language. To give their answers, the participants are instructed to use the arrows on the keyboard. For half of the participants, the left arrow corresponds to “yes”, and the right one to “no”, while the other half of the participants receives the opposite instructions. 

The task is preceded by a consent form at the beginning of the experiment. After the consent form, the instructions appear on the screen, followed by 10 practice trials. Feedback is provided during the practice trials. The participants are then notified that the practice is over, and that feedback will not be provided from then on, after which they can start the experiment. The main experiment contains 480 trials divided into 4 blocks with 120 trials each. A break is given after each block. At the beginning of each trial, a fixation cross appears for 500 ms, followed by the stimulus that stays on the screen for 2.5 seconds or until the participant answers. A blank screen between the stimuli is also added with the duration of 1000 ms. After the last trial, a short debriefing is presented, describing the aims of the experiment, and offering the opportunity to leave comments. The last part of the experiment is a language questionnaire. The questionnaire includes questions about the participants’ native language(s), country of birth and schooling, and other questions that might be relevant for understanding the participant language profile (see below in Other).
table.randomization: Each participant will randomly be assigned to a list in which the “yes” answer is on the left, or a version where “yes” is on the right side¬, using Balanced Randomization mode to an ensure equal number of participants per version. Moreover, trials at each run will be randomized using the randomise_trials column in the Gorilla spreadsheet, so that the order of the item presentation is different for each participant.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: The recruitment will be done via Prolific (https://www.prolific.co/). We will screen participants for age (over 18), native/first language (Tagalog), city where they originated from in the Philippines, and device (desktop or laptop, but not tablet or mobile). Participants will be directed to the study on Gorilla. At the end of the experiment, they will be directed back to Prolific. Participants will be remunerated the equivalent of £7.50/hr for their participation via the Prolific platform (the experiment takes between 20 and 30 minutes).
table.sample_size: An initial sample of 70 participants will be recruited in this experiment. We will then determine which proportion of primes for each participant was recorded by Gorilla as being presented for the target duration (33ms), and which proportion were recorded as presented for longer. Primes presented for longer than 60ms (the upper limit for masked priming effects reported in the literature) will be flagged. If 10% or more of primes for a participant exceed 60ms, that participant will be excluded from analysis and additional participants will be recruited until we have 70 participants with 90% prime duration accuracy and 80% accuracy on the critical trials. A complete analysis of the data will then be undertaken.
table.sample_size_rationale: We will be recruiting 70 native Tagalog speakers. The sample size is designed to follow the previous masked affix priming experiment we conducted in Gorilla, where we successfully replicated robust priming effects for prime-target pairs that share the same affix, while no such effects were found for prime-target pairs that share non-morphological orthographic overlap.
table.stopping_rule: If the target results are not replicated with 70 participants (see Hypothesis section), the study will be terminated.
table.manipulated_variables: The variables that are manipulated for the experiment are Relation Type and Prime Type. The Relation Type variable controls the types of morphological relationship between the prime and the target, which can either be morphologically related (in-INF/ʔ-INF, ʔ-INF/in-INF, ʔ-INF/ni-PREF, in-INF/ni-PREF, in-INF-same-pos) or orthographically related (OrthCont). The Prime Type variable controls the relatedness between the prime and the target, which can be related (morphologically and orthographically) or completely unrelated.
table.measured_variables: Participants’ Reaction Time (RT) to targets when preceded by the related and unrelated primes will be compared in this study (see Analysis Plan). Participants’ lexical decision accuracy on each trial will determine whether that trial is included or excluded, and participant accuracy rates will determine whether a participant is included or excluded (see Exclusion Criteria).
table.statistical_tests:
We will use Mixed-Effects regression analyses in the lme4 package in R. The model will have Reaction Time (RT) as the dependent variable and RelationType (in-INF/ʔ-INF, ʔ-INF/in-INF, ʔ-INF/ni-PREF, in-INF/ni-PREF, in-INF-same-pos, and OrthCont) crossed with PrimeType (related, unrelated) as fixed effects. The baseline level for PrimeType will be ‘Unrelated’. For RelationType, the baseline will first be ʔ-INF/in-INF to allow comparison with the reversed condition in-INF/ʔ-INF. We will then set the baseline to ni-PREF/ʔ-INF to allow comparison with ni-PREF/in-INF. By-subject and by-item random slopes and intercepts will be included as random effects. The initial full model will be coded as: TagPrime ← lmer(RT ~ RelationType * PrimeType + (RelationType*PrimeType|Subject) + (RelationType*PrimeType|Item), REML = F). To choose the best random effects structure, Log-likelihood ratio testing will be used. We will compare models with by-subject and by-item random slopes to the model with only a by-subject random slope. If the less complicated model is more parsimonious based on BIC and AIC, then we will simplify the model by dropping the random slope for items. The same process will be applied to by-subject random slope. 

The full model with RelationType * PrimeType interaction will be compared to the model without interaction RelationType + PrimeType. If the less complex model has better goodness of fit, the model will be further simplified by removing RelationType as a factor and compared to the model with this factor. Since the critical criterion for assessing whether we get masked priming effects is obtaining significant priming in the ʔ-INF/in-INF, in-INF/ʔ-INF, ni-PREF/ʔ-INF, ni-PREF/in-INF, in-INF-same-pos, but no significant OrthCont priming, the RelationType is the most important factor. If RelationType does not make a significant contribution to the model’s goodness of fit, we will consider that we have failed to find the effect.

Multiple comparison corrections will be done using the emmeans package in R, particularly Tukey HSD, which will be coded as: TagPrime.emm = emmans(TagPrime, ~ RelationType * PrimeType), then pairs(TagPrime.emm, simple = “each”). This will generate simple main-effect contrast sets, comparing the magnitude of RelationType * PrimeType interaction effects across conditions.
table.inference_criteria: We will be using the T value >|2| criteria to evaluate significance in our linear mixed models. We are also expecting an effect size of > 20ms for the in-INF/ʔ-INF, ʔ-INF/in-INF, ʔ-INF/ni-PREF, in-INF/ni-PREF, and in-INF-same-pos priming effect, which is the effect size commonly reported in masked affix priming literature (see Crepaldi et al., 2015).
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Prior to data analysis, participant error rates for the grammatical items will be calculated. Participants rejecting more than 20% of the grammatical items will be excluded from analysis. Participants who don’t list Tagalog as of their native language, and who attended primary and secondary school outside of the Philippines will be removed.

Only accurate response data will be included in the RT analyses. We will first remove responses shorter than 200 ms. Further outlier removal will be performed following Baayen and Millin (2010), by fitting a simple mixed model with only random effects and excluding all data points with residuals exceeding 2.5 SD.
table.missing_data_handling: The lmer function in R removes the missing data.

table.title: Does affix linear position matter during morpheme detection process? Evidence from a Tagalog masked affix priming experiment
table.research_questions:
If affixes are actively processed during morphological processing and are represented in the human mind, then we expect to find robust priming effects for -in- INF, -um- INF, ni- PREF, and ʔ-INF conditions, where the prime-target pairs share the same affix. These findings would be consistent with previous masked affix priming studies in English (Chateau et al., 2002, Crepaldi et al., 2015, Duñabeitia et al., 2008), French (Giraudo & Grainger, 2003), Spanish (Dominguez et al., 2010), Maltese (Ussishkin et al., 2015), and Arabic (Boudelaa & Marslen-Wilson, 2005).

Moreover, if these priming effects are truly morphological, then no such facilitation should be observed for monomorphemic prime-target pairs with non-morphological orthographic overlap (e.g., lampin-LAMBAT ‘diaper-NET’). 

If affix linear position affects morphological detection process, then we predict to find less robust priming effects for -in- INF and -um- INF conditions than ni-PREF and potentially ʔ-INF conditions. This would be consistent with models like “beginning-to-end” sequential bias (see Diependaele et al., 2009). Importantly, ʔ-INF condition may behave like a prefix since it is orthographically left-edge aligned or like an infix due to being phonologically non-edge aligned. Tagalog allows us to tease these possibilities apart.

Finally, if a viable stem is required to trigger form-based decomposition mechanisms (see Gwilliams & Marantz, 2018), then no priming effects should be obtained for -in- Pseudo-INF and -um- Pseudo-INF conditions. This would contract the previous Tagalog neuroimaging study of Wray et al. (2022).

The last part of the experiment is a language questionnaire. The questionnaire includes questions about the participants’ native language(s), country of birth and schooling, and other questions that might be relevant for understanding the participant language profile (see below in Other).
table.randomization: Each participant will randomly be assigned to a list in which the “yes” answer is on the left, or a version where “yes” is on the right side¬, using Balanced Randomization mode to an ensure equal number of participants per version. Moreover, trials at each run will be randomized using the randomise_trials column in the Gorilla spreadsheet, so that the order of the item presentation is different for each participant.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: The recruitment will be done via Prolific (https://www.prolific.co/). We will screen participants for age (over 18), native/first language (Tagalog), city where they originated from the Philippines, and device (desktop or laptop, but not tablet or mobile). Participants will be directed to the study on Gorilla. At the end of the experiment, they will be directed back to Prolific. Participants will be renumerated the equivalent of £7.50/hr for their participation via the Prolific platform (the experiment takes between 20 and 30 minutes).
table.sample_size: Data collection will be done using sequential samples. An initial sample of 40 participants will be recruited. We will then determine which proportion of primes for each participant was recorded by Gorilla as being presented for the intended duration (33ms), and which proportion were recorded as presented for longer. Primes presented for longer than 60ms (the upper limit for masked priming effects reported in the literature) will be flagged. If 10% or more of primes for a participant exceed 60ms, that participant will be excluded from analysis and additional participants will be recruited until we have 40 participants with 90% prime duration accuracy. A complete analysis of the data will then be undertaken. Another set of 40 participants will be recruited and the data will go through the same pre-processing stages and analyses.
table.sample_size_rationale: The initial sample size is designed to follow the previous masked priming experiment we conducted in Gorilla, where we successfully replicated masked morphological priming effects with 80 participants. However, it has to be noted that the current experiment has a more fine-grained morphological relatedness (only sharing an affix), rather than a simple stem overlap. The sequential sampling plan, up to a maximum of 120 participants, is motivated both by research comparing Internet-based data to lab-based data, which has shown that the data quality is similar as long as the Internet-based sample size is at least three times larger than the lab-based sample size (Gosling et al., 2004). The number of participants in the lab-based experiments employing lexical decision task from the previous studies varies between 20 and 46 (Manouilidou, 2007; Manouilidou & Stockall, 2014, Neophytou et al 2018, Stockall et al 2019), so we considered 80-120 to be an appropriate number for an online masked affix priming experiment.
table.stopping_rule: Depending on the findings, we will either stop or run one more set of 40 participants, then analyze their RT again, again excluding and replacing participants with >10% prime duration error. If the target results are not replicated with 120 participants (see Hypothesis section), the study will be terminated.
table.manipulated_variables:
The variables that are manipulated for the experiment are Relation Type and Prime Type. The Relation Type variable controls the types of relationship between the prime and the target, which can either be truly morphologically related (e.g., -in- INF, -um- INF, ni- PREF, and ʔ-INF), pseudo morphologically related (-in- Pseudo-INF, -um- Pseudo-INF), or orthographically related (Orth.Con). The Prime Type variable controls the relatedness between the prime and the target, which can be related (morphologically, pseudo-morphologically, or orthographically) or completely unrelated. 

We also added filler items, which do not form part of the main analysis.
table.measured_variables: Participants’ Reaction Time (RT) to the target when preceded by related and unrelated primes will be compared in this study (see Analysis Plan). Participants’ lexical decision accuracy on each trial will determine whether that trial is included or excluded, and participant accuracy rates will determine whether a participant is included or excluded (see Exclusion Criteria).
table.statistical_tests:
We will use Mixed-Effects regression analyses in the lme4 package in R. The model will have Reaction Time (RT) as the dependent variable and RelationType (-in- INF, -um- INF, ni- PREF, ʔ-INF, -in- Pseudo-INF, -um- Pseudo-INF, Orth.Con) crossed with PrimeType (related, unrelated) as fixed effects. The baseline levels for the two fixed factors will be ‘-in- INF’ and ‘unrelated’, respectively. By-subject and by-item random slopes and intercepts will be included as random effects. The initial full model will be coded as: TagPrime ← lmer(RT ~ RelationType * PrimeType + (RelationType*PrimeType|Subject) + (RelationType*PrimeType|Item), REML = F). To choose the best random effects structure, Log-likelihood ratio testing will be used. We will compare models with by-subject and by-item random slopes to the model with only a by-subject random slope. If the less complicated model is more parsimonious based on BIC and AIC, then we will simplify the model by dropping the random slope for items. The same process will be applied to by-subject random slope. 

The full model with RelationType * PrimeType interaction will be compared to the model without interaction RelationType + PrimeType. If the less complex model has better goodness of fit, the model will be further simplified by removing RelationType as a factor and compared to the model with this factor. Since the critical criterion for assessing whether we get masked priming effects is obtaining significant priming in -in- INF, -um- INF, ni- PREF, and ʔ-INF (potentially -in- Pseudo-INF, -um- Pseudo-INF), but no significant Orth.Con priming, the RelationType is the most important factor. If RelationType does not make a significant contribution to the model’s goodness of fit, we will consider that we have failed to find the effect.

We will also run separate analyses where the -in- Pseudo-INF and -um- Pseudo-INF conditions will be collapsed into one condition Pseudo-INF to further investigate the decomposition of pseudo-infixed words. 

Multiple comparison corrections will be done using the emmeans package in R, particularly Tukey HSD, which will be coded as: TagPrime.emm = emmans(TagPrime, ~ RelationType * PrimeType), then pairs(TagPrime.emm, simple = “each”). This will generate simple main-effect contrast sets, comparing the magnitude of RelationType * PrimeType interaction effects across conditions.
table.inference_criteria: We will be using the T value >|2| criteria to evaluate significance in our linear mixed models. We are also expecting an effect size of > 20ms for the -in- INF, -um- INF, ni PREF, and ʔ-INF priming effect, which is the effect size commonly reported in masked affix priming literature (see Crepaldi et al., 2015).
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Prior to data analysis, participant error rates for the grammatical items will be calculated. Participants rejecting more than 20% of the real word items will be excluded from analysis. Participants who don’t list Tagalog as of their native language, and who attended primary and secondary school outside of the Philippines will be removed.

Only accurate response data will be included in the RT analyses. We will first remove responses shorter than 200 ms. Further outlier removal will be performed following Baayen and Millin (2010), by fitting a simple mixed model with only random effects and excluding all data points with residuals exceeding 2.5 SD.
table.missing_data_handling: The lmer function in R removes the missing data.
