This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.", "For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.", "Design and materials

This masked affix priming experiment will be conducted in Gorilla.sc, an online experiment platform, and Tagalog speakers will be recruited as participants via Prolific.

In this experiment, there will be four conditions, where the affixes in the prime and the target are in different orthographic linear positions: [1](a) the ʔ infix cross-position (in-INF/ʔ-INF) condition presents a target word with an -in- infix attached to a glottal stop initial stem (e.g., INUBOS from /ʔubos/ ‘consumed’) preceded by an -in- infixed word prime with the -in- following a written consonant (e.g., tinali ‘tied’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., kumuda ‘talked’) & [1](b) (ʔ-INF/in-INF) where the prime-target direction is reversed; [2](a) the ni- prefix/-in- infix (in-INF/ni-PREF) cross-position condition presents a ni- prefixed word as a target (e.g., NIYUKO ‘bowed’) preceded by an -in- infixed word prime (e.g., binali ‘broke’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., lumagi ‘stay’) & [2](b) ʔ-INF/ni-PREF where the ni- prefixed target word is preceded by an -in- infix attached to a glottal stop initial stem (inalis-NIYUKO ‘removed-BOWED’). All unrelated primes are morphologically complex words with a different affix (i.e., -um- infix). The affixes in the related primes and unrelated primes are matched for orthographic length and linear position. There will be 40 trials in each condition.

There will also be two baseline conditions: a same position condition and an orthographic control condition, with 40 trials each. The -in- infix same position (ʔ-INF-same-pos) condition presents an -in- infixed target word attached to a glottal stop initial stem (e.g., INAYOS ‘fixed’) preceded by a prime with -in- infix appearing orthographically in the same prefix position (e.g., inusog ‘pushed’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., umandar ‘to move’). The orthographic control condition (OrthCont) consists of monomorphemic prime-target words with orthographic overlap in the first three letters (lampin-LAMBAT ‘diaper-NET’, bunyag-BUNDOL ‘reveal-HIT LIGHTLY’) and monomorphemic unrelated primes, which are words that have no orthographic overlap in the first three letters as the target (e.g., bughaw-LAMBAT ‘blue-NET’, pigtas-BUNDOL ‘break off-HIT LIGHTLY’). The overlap in the related condition is in the first three-letters, as the orthographic overlap in the critical conditions is also in that position.

The items for the morphologically related conditions were selected by generating a large candidate set of morphologically complex words with the infix -in-, prefix ni-, and the -in- infix attached to glottal stop initial stems. As a second step, only infixed and prefixed words with 5-8 letters and with whole word frequency above 0.05 per million were retained in the candidate sets. Target words were pairwise matched with related and unrelated primes for orthographic length. To generate unrelated prime words, we generated a large candidate set of -um- infixed words that are 5-8 letters long with a lexical frequency of above 0.05 per million. Unrelated primes were pairwise matched with related primes for orthographic length and whole word lexical frequency. Due to limited items, the related primes in the in-INF/ʔ-INF condition were repeated as targets in the ʔ-INF/in-INF condition. Moreover, the related primes in the ʔ-IN/ni-PREF condition were repeated as targets in the ʔ-INF-same-pos condition. Some unrelated primes in the ʔ-INF/ni-PREF condition were also repeated as unrelated primes in the ʔ-INF-same-pos condition. To reduce long-lag priming, these repeated items were separated into different blocks, making a total of 4 blocks in this experiment.

To generate items for the orthographic control condition, the first author, who is a native Tagalog speaker, created word pairs with first three-letter overlap (e.g., lampin-LAMBAT ‘diaper-NET’, bunyag-BUNDOL ‘reveal-HIT LIGHTLY’). Monomorphemic words were assigned as an unrelated prime if they had no orthographic overlap in the first three letters with the target word. Only words that are 4-8 letters long with a lexical frequency above 0.05 per million were retained from the candidate set. As a second step, Levenshtein distance (Levenshtein, 1965) was used to derive an orthographic overlap score. Only word pairs with a Levenshtein score of <4 were included in the related condition, while word pairs with a Levenshtein score of >5 were included in the unrelated condition.

Lexical frequencies were obtained from SketchEngine, an online platform that compiles web-based text corpora from more than 900 languages. The most recent version of the Tagalog corpus in this platform has 198, 303, 250 words. The targets in the ʔ-INF/in-INF, in-INF/ʔ-INF, ni-PREF/ʔ-INF, ni-PREF/ʔ-INF, in-INF-same-pos, and OrthCont conditions were list-wise matched as close as possible for orthographic length and lexical frequency. Further, the related and unrelated primes were pairwise and list-wise matched as close as possible for lexical frequency and orthographic length. The same matching were employed in the OrthCont condition. All targets and primes in the final stimulus list are words with frequencies above 0.05 per million in SketchEngine. Since primes and targets both range in length between 4-8 characters, a forward mask of 8 #s were chosen to ensure complete masking of all primes, and that no cue to prime or target length is provided by the mask. A proportional font, in which each character takes up the same amount of space, were used to ensure the forward mask completely covers the same visual range as the prime, and that the prime and target extend over the same visual range.

A set of nonword primes and targets were generated using the pseudoword generator toolkit Wuggy by scrambling possible syllables using real Tagalog words as training input (Keuleers & Brysbaert, 2010). In Wuggy, the real word training inputs and the nonword outputs were matched in length of subsyllabic segments, letter length, and transition frequencies (i.e., the number of words in which two specific subsyllabic elements occur in sequence). A total of 240 nonword targets and 120 nonwords primes were selected in the final stimulus list to serve as filler trials. All nonword primes and targets that were selected are pronounceable nonwords ranging between 4-8 characters to match the critical and control trials. The other half of the nonword targets were preceded by real word primes to avoid cueing participants to the lexical decision they should make. The real word primes are 6-8 characters long. Both nonword and real word primes were list-wise and pairwise matched for orthographic length. Moreover, both real word and nonword primes were pairwise matched to the targets for orthographic length to match the critical and control conditions.

This resulted in a total of 240 trials (120 related and 120 unrelated) in this experiment, which were pseudo-interleaved with 240 filler trials, consisting of 120 nonword-nonword (NW-NW) prime-target pairs (e.g., dukmo-BABAG) and 120 word-nonword (W-NW) pairs (e.g., hiling-BALTAY 'request'-BALTAY). We created 10 practice trials. Overall, the entire experiment consists of 490 trials.

The masked prime will be presented for 33ms, following previous masked affix priming experiments. The primes will be masked by being preceded by strings of number signs (e.g., ########) for 500ms. The forward mask will be preceded by a fixation cross for 500ms. Native Tagalog speakers will have 2500ms to judge whether the target word is a real Tagalog word or not by pressing the corresponding arrow key. If no response is registered, the experiment will automatically proceed to the next trial. Participants will be continuously cued by TUNAY ‘Yes’ and HINDI ‘No’ on opposite sides of the screen. For half of the participants, TUNAY maps to the left arrow key and HINDI maps to the right arrow key, while the other half will apply the opposite mappings. Overall, a complete trial sequence is as follows: [+ for 500ms] [######## for 500ms] [prime for 33ms] [TARGET for 2500ms or until button press] [ISI 1000ms]. Targets will be presented in upper case, and primes in lower case - the case change is necessary to create a visual change between the prime and target in the critical condition.

The experiment is a within-subject design - all participants will see the critical targets in both their related prime and unrelated prime condition. The two occurrences of each target will be separated in different blocks, with a short break in between. The order of items within a block will be pseudo-randomised for each participant, and the order of the four blocks will be permuted across participants such that each block occurs as the first block for ¼ of participants. Participants will be randomly assigned to each experimental list.

Procedure

The experiment consists of a lexical decision task in which participants are presented with strings of letters appearing in the middle of the screen, and their task is to say whether a string is an existing word of their native language. To give their answers, the participants are instructed to use the arrows on the keyboard. For half of the participants, the left arrow corresponds to “yes”, and the right one to “no”, while the other half of the participants receives the opposite instructions.

The task is preceded by a consent form at the beginning of the experiment. After the consent form, the instructions appear on the screen, followed by 10 practice trials. Feedback is provided during the practice trials. The participants are then notified that the practice is over, and that feedback will not be provided from then on, after which they can start the experiment. The main experiment contains 480 trials divided into 4 blocks with 120 trials each. A break is given after each block. At the beginning of each trial, a fixation cross appears for 500 ms, followed by the stimulus that stays on the screen for 2.5 seconds or until the participant answers. A blank screen between the stimuli is also added with the duration of 1000 ms. After the last trial, a short debriefing is presented, describing the aims of the experiment, and offering the opportunity to leave comments. The last part of the experiment is a language questionnaire. The items for -in- INF, -um- INF, ni- PREF, and ʔ-INF conditions will be selected by generating a large candidate set of morphologically complex words with the infixes -in-, -um-, and the prefix ni-. Unrelated primes will be pairwise matched with related primes for orthographic length and lexical frequency.

These monomorphemic target words can also be preceded by unrelated primes, which are words that have no overlap in the first three letters as the target (e.g., bughaw-LAMBAT ‘blue-NET’, pigtas-BUNDOL ‘break off-HIT LIGHTLY’). Related and unrelated primes will be pairwise and list-wise matched as close as possible for lexical frequency. The same matching will be employed in the Orth.Con condition. The masked prime will be presented for 33ms. The primes will be masked by being preceded by strings of number signs (e.g., ########) for 500ms. Procedure

The experiment consists of a lexical decision task in which participants are presented with strings of letters appearing in the middle of the screen, and their task is to say whether a string is an existing word of their native language. To give their answers, the participants are instructed to use the arrows on the keyboard. For half of the participants, the left arrow corresponds to “yes”, and the right one to “no”, while the other half of the participants receives the opposite instructions.

The task is preceded by a consent form at the beginning of the experiment. After the consent form, the instructions appear on the screen, followed by 10 practice trials. Feedback is provided during the practice trials. The participants are then notified that the practice is over, and that feedback will not be provided from then on, after which they can start the experiment. The main experiment contains 528 trials, with a break half-way through after 264 trials. At the beginning of each trial, a fixation cross appears for 500 ms, followed by the stimulus that stays on the screen for 2.5 seconds or until the participant answers. A blank screen between the stimuli is also added with the duration of 1000ms. After the last trial, a short debriefing is presented, describing the aims of the experiment, and offering the opportunity to leave comments. The last part of the experiment is a language questionnaire. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.", "For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.", "Design and materials

This masked affix priming experiment will be conducted in Gorilla.sc, an online experiment platform, and Tagalog speakers will be recruited as participants via Prolific.

In this experiment, there will be four conditions, where the affixes in the prime and the target are in different orthographic linear positions: [1](a) the ʔ infix cross-position (in-INF/ʔ-INF) condition presents a target word with an -in- infix attached to a glottal stop initial stem (e.g., INUBOS from /ʔubos/ ‘consumed’) preceded by an -in- infixed word prime with the -in- following a written consonant (e.g., tinali ‘tied’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., kumuda ‘talked’) & [1](b) (ʔ-INF/in-INF) where the prime-target direction is reversed; [2](a) the ni- prefix/-in- infix (in-INF/ni-PREF) cross-position condition presents a ni- prefixed word as a target (e.g., NIYUKO ‘bowed’) preceded by an -in- infixed word prime (e.g., binali ‘broke’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., lumagi ‘stay’) & [2](b) ʔ-INF/ni-PREF where the ni- prefixed target word is preceded by an -in- infix attached to a glottal stop initial stem (inalis-NIYUKO ‘removed-BOWED’). All unrelated primes are morphologically complex words with a different affix (i.e., -um- infix). The affixes in the related primes and unrelated primes are matched for orthographic length and linear position. There will be 40 trials in each condition.

There will also be two baseline conditions: a same position condition and an orthographic control condition, with 40 trials each. The -in- infix same position (ʔ-INF-same-pos) condition presents an -in- infixed target word attached to a glottal stop initial stem (e.g., INAYOS ‘fixed’) preceded by a prime with -in- infix appearing orthographically in the same prefix position (e.g., inusog ‘pushed’) or an unrelated prime (e.g., umandar ‘to move’). The orthographic control condition (OrthCont) consists of monomorphemic prime-target words with orthographic overlap in the first three letters (lampin-LAMBAT ‘diaper-NET’, bunyag-BUNDOL ‘reveal-HIT LIGHTLY’) and monomorphemic unrelated primes, which are words that have no orthographic overlap in the first three letters as the target (e.g., bughaw-LAMBAT ‘blue-NET’, pigtas-BUNDOL ‘break off-HIT LIGHTLY’). The overlap in the related condition is in the first three-letters, as the orthographic overlap in the critical conditions is also in that position.

The items for the morphologically related conditions were selected by generating a large candidate set of morphologically complex words with the infix -in-, prefix ni-, and the -in- infix attached to glottal stop initial stems. As a second step, only infixed and prefixed words with 5-8 letters and with whole word frequency above 0.05 per million were retained in the candidate sets. Target words were pairwise matched with related and unrelated primes for orthographic length. To generate unrelated prime words, we generated a large candidate set of -um- infixed words that are 5-8 letters long with a lexical frequency of above 0.05 per million. Unrelated primes were pairwise matched with related primes for orthographic length and whole word lexical frequency. Due to limited items, the related primes in the in-INF/ʔ-INF condition were repeated as targets in the ʔ-INF/in-INF condition. Moreover, the related primes in the ʔ-IN/ni-PREF condition were repeated as targets in the ʔ-INF-same-pos condition. Some unrelated primes in the ʔ-INF/ni-PREF condition were also repeated as unrelated primes in the ʔ-INF-same-pos condition. To reduce long-lag priming, these repeated items were separated into different blocks, making a total of 4 blocks in this experiment.

To generate items for the orthographic control condition, the first author, who is a native Tagalog speaker, created word pairs with first three-letter overlap (e.g., lampin-LAMBAT ‘diaper-NET’, bunyag-BUNDOL ‘reveal-HIT LIGHTLY’). Monomorphemic words were assigned as an unrelated prime if they had no orthographic overlap in the first three letters with the target word. Only words that are 4-8 letters long with a lexical frequency above 0.05 per million were retained from the candidate set. As a second step, Levenshtein distance (Levenshtein, 1965) was used to derive an orthographic overlap score. Only word pairs with a Levenshtein score of <4 were included in the related condition, while word pairs with a Levenshtein score of >5 were included in the unrelated condition.

Lexical frequencies were obtained from SketchEngine, an online platform that compiles web-based text corpora from more than 900 languages. The most recent version of the Tagalog corpus in this platform has 198, 303, 250 words. The targets in the ʔ-INF/in-INF, in-INF/ʔ-INF, ni-PREF/ʔ-INF, ni-PREF/ʔ-INF, in-INF-same-pos, and OrthCont conditions were list-wise matched as close as possible for orthographic length and lexical frequency. Further, the related and unrelated primes were pairwise and list-wise matched as close as possible for lexical frequency and orthographic length. The same matching were employed in the OrthCont condition. All targets and primes in the final stimulus list are words with frequencies above 0.05 per million in SketchEngine. Since primes and targets both range in length between 4-8 characters, a forward mask of 8 #s were chosen to ensure complete masking of all primes, and that no cue to prime or target length is provided by the mask. A proportional font, in which each character takes up the same amount of space, were used to ensure the forward mask completely covers the same visual range as the prime, and that the prime and target extend over the same visual range.

A set of nonword primes and targets were generated using the pseudoword generator toolkit Wuggy by scrambling possible syllables using real Tagalog words as training input (Keuleers & Brysbaert, 2010). In Wuggy, the real word training inputs and the nonword outputs were matched in length of subsyllabic segments, letter length, and transition frequencies (i.e., the number of words in which two specific subsyllabic elements occur in sequence). A total of 240 nonword targets and 120 nonwords primes were selected in the final stimulus list to serve as filler trials. All nonword primes and targets that were selected are pronounceable nonwords ranging between 4-8 characters to match the critical and control trials. The other half of the nonword targets were preceded by real word primes to avoid cueing participants to the lexical decision they should make. The real word primes are 6-8 characters long. Both nonword and real word primes were list-wise and pairwise matched for orthographic length. Moreover, both real word and nonword primes were pairwise matched to the targets for orthographic length to match the critical and control conditions.

This resulted in a total of 240 trials (120 related and 120 unrelated) in this experiment, which were pseudo-interleaved with 240 filler trials, consisting of 120 nonword-nonword (NW-NW) prime-target pairs (e.g., dukmo-BABAG) and 120 word-nonword (W-NW) pairs (e.g., hiling-BALTAY 'request'-BALTAY). We created 10 practice trials. Overall, the entire experiment consists of 490 trials.

The masked prime will be presented for 33ms, following previous masked affix priming experiments. The primes will be masked by being preceded by strings of number signs (e.g., ########) for 500ms. The forward mask will be preceded by a fixation cross for 500ms. Native Tagalog speakers will have 2500ms to judge whether the target word is a real Tagalog word or not by pressing the corresponding arrow key. If no response is registered, the experiment will automatically proceed to the next trial. Participants will be continuously cued by TUNAY ‘Yes’ and HINDI ‘No’ on opposite sides of the screen. For half of the participants, TUNAY maps to the left arrow key and HINDI maps to the right arrow key, while the other half will apply the opposite mappings. Overall, a complete trial sequence is as follows: [+ for 500ms] [######## for 500ms] [prime for 33ms] [TARGET for 2500ms or until button press] [ISI 1000ms]. Targets will be presented in upper case, and primes in lower case - the case change is necessary to create a visual change between the prime and target in the critical condition.

The experiment is a within-subject design - all participants will see the critical targets in both their related prime and unrelated prime condition. The two occurrences of each target will be separated in different blocks, with a short break in between. The order of items within a block will be pseudo-randomised for each participant, and the order of the four blocks will be permuted across participants such that each block occurs as the first block for ¼ of participants. Participants will be randomly assigned to each experimental list.

Procedure

The experiment consists of a lexical decision task in which participants are presented with strings of letters appearing in the middle of the screen, and their task is to say whether a string is an existing word of their native language. To give their answers, the participants are instructed to use the arrows on the keyboard. For half of the participants, the left arrow corresponds to “yes”, and the right one to “no”, while the other half of the participants receives the opposite instructions.

The task is preceded by a consent form at the beginning of the experiment. After the consent form, the instructions appear on the screen, followed by 10 practice trials. Feedback is provided during the practice trials. The participants are then notified that the practice is over, and that feedback will not be provided from then on, after which they can start the experiment. The main experiment contains 480 trials divided into 4 blocks with 120 trials each. A break is given after each block. At the beginning of each trial, a fixation cross appears for 500 ms, followed by the stimulus that stays on the screen for 2.5 seconds or until the participant answers. A blank screen between the stimuli is also added with the duration of 1000 ms. After the last trial, a short debriefing is presented, describing the aims of the experiment, and offering the opportunity to leave comments. The last part of the experiment is a language questionnaire. The questionnaire includes questions about the participants’ native language(s), country of birth and schooling, and other questions that might be relevant for understanding the participant language profile (see below in Other).", "Each participant will randomly be assigned to a list in which the “yes” answer is on the left, or a version where “yes” is on the right side¬, using Balanced Randomization mode to an ensure equal number of participants per version. Since primes and targets both range in length between 4-8 characters, a forward mask of 8 #s will be chosen to ensure complete masking of all primes, and that no cue to prime or target length is provided by the mask. A proportional font, in which each character takes up the same amount of space, will be used to ensure the forward mask completely covers the same visual range as the prime, and that the prime and target extend over the same visual range.

A set of nonword primes and targets will be generated using the pseudoword generator toolkit Wuggy by scrambling possible syllables using real Tagalog words as training input (Keuleers & Brysbaert, 2010). In Wuggy, the real word training inputs and the nonword outputs will be matched in length of subsyllabic segments, letter length, and transition frequencies (i.e., the number of words in which two specific subsyllabic elements occur in sequence). A total of 264 nonword targets and 132 nonwords primes will be selected in the final stimulus list to serve as filler trials. All nonword primes and targets that will be selected are pronounceable nonwords ranging between 4-8 characters to match the critical and control trials. The other half of the nonword targets will be preceded by real word primes to avoid cueing participants to the lexical decision they should make. The real word primes are 4-8 characters long. Both nonword and real word primes will be list-wise matched for orthographic length. Moreover, both real word and nonword primes will be pairwise matched with their nonword target for orthographic length to match the critical and control conditions.

The masked prime will be presented for 33ms. The primes will be masked by being preceded by strings of number signs (e.g., ########) for 500ms. The forward mask will be preceded by a fixation cross for 500ms. Native Tagalog speakers will have 2500ms to judge whether the target word is a real Tagalog word or not by pressing the corresponding arrow key. If no response is registered, the experiment will automatically proceed to the next trial. Participants will be continuously cued by TUNAY ‘Yes’ and HINDI ‘No’ on opposite sides of the screen. For half of the participants, TUNAY maps to the left arrow key and HINDI maps to the right arrow key, while the other half will apply the opposite mappings. Overall, a complete trial sequence is as follows: [+ for 500ms] [######## for 500ms] [prime for 33ms] [TARGET for 2500ms or until button press] [ISI 1000ms]. Targets will be presented in upper case, and primes in lower case - the case change is necessary to create a visual change between the prime and target in the critical condition.

The experiment is a within-subject design - all participants will see the critical targets in both their related prime and unrelated prime conditions. The two occurrences of each target will be separated into two separate blocks, with a short break in between. The order of items within a block will be pseudo-randomised for each participant, and the order of the two blocks will be permuted across participants such that each block occurs as the first block for 1/2 of participants and as the second block for the other half.

Procedure

The experiment consists of a lexical decision task in which participants are presented with strings of letters appearing in the middle of the screen, and their task is to say whether a string is an existing word of their native language. To give their answers, the participants are instructed to use the arrows on the keyboard. For half of the participants, the left arrow corresponds to “yes”, and the right one to “no”, while the other half of the participants receives the opposite instructions.

The task is preceded by a consent form at the beginning of the experiment. After the consent form, the instructions appear on the screen, followed by 10 practice trials. Feedback is provided during the practice trials. The participants are then notified that the practice is over, and that feedback will not be provided from then on, after which they can start the experiment. The main experiment contains 528 trials, with a break half-way through after 264 trials. At the beginning of each trial, a fixation cross appears for 500 ms, followed by the stimulus that stays on the screen for 2.5 seconds or until the participant answers. A blank screen between the stimuli is also added with the duration of 1000ms. After the last trial, a short debriefing is presented, describing the aims of the experiment, and offering the opportunity to leave comments. The last part of the experiment is a language questionnaire. The questionnaire includes questions about the participants’ native language(s), country of birth and schooling, and other questions that might be relevant for understanding the participant language profile (see below in Other).", "Each participant will randomly be assigned to a list in which the “yes” answer is on the left, or a version where “yes” is on the right side¬, using Balanced Randomization mode to an ensure equal number of participants per version. Moreover, trials at each run will be randomized using the randomise_trials column in the Gorilla spreadsheet, so that the order of the item presentation is different for each participant.", "Registration prior to creation of data", "The recruitment will be done via Prolific (https://www.prolific.co/). We will screen participants for age (over 18), native/first language (Tagalog), city where they originated from the Philippines, and device (desktop or laptop, but not tablet or mobile). Participants will be directed to the study on Gorilla. At the end of the experiment, they will be directed back to Prolific. Participants will be renumerated the equivalent of £7.50/hr for their participation via the Prolific platform (the experiment takes between 20 and 30 minutes).", "Data collection will be done using sequential samples. An initial sample of 40 participants will be recruited. We will then determine which proportion of primes for each participant was recorded by Gorilla as being presented for the intended duration (33ms), and which proportion were recorded as presented for longer. Primes presented for longer than 60ms (the upper limit for masked priming effects reported in the literature) will be flagged. If 10% or more of primes for a participant exceed 60ms, that participant will be excluded from analysis and additional participants will be recruited until we have 40 participants with 90% prime duration accuracy. A complete analysis of the data will then be undertaken. Another set of 40 participants will be recruited and the data will go through the same pre-processing stages and analyses.", "The initial sample size is designed to follow the previous masked priming experiment we conducted in Gorilla, where we successfully replicated masked morphological priming effects with 80 participants. However, it has to be noted that the current experiment has a more fine-grained morphological relatedness (only sharing an affix), rather than a simple stem overlap. The sequential sampling plan, up to a maximum of 120 participants, is motivated both by research comparing Internet-based data to lab-based data, which has shown that the data quality is similar as long as the Internet-based sample size is at least three times larger than the lab-based sample size (Gosling et al., 2004). The number of participants in the lab-based experiments employing lexical decision task from the previous studies varies between 20 and 46 (Manouilidou, 2007; Manouilidou & Stockall, 2014, Neophytou et al 2018, Stockall et al 2019), so we considered 80-120 to be an appropriate number for an online masked affix priming experiment.", "Depending on the findings, we will either stop or run one more set of 40 participants, then analyze their RT again, again excluding and replacing participants with >10% prime duration error. If the target results are not replicated with 120 participants (see Hypothesis section), the study will be terminated.", "The variables that are manipulated for the experiment are Relation Type and Prime Type. The Relation Type variable controls the types of relationship between the prime and the target, which can either be truly morphologically related (e.g., -in- INF, -um- INF, ni- PREF, and ʔ-INF), pseudo morphologically related (-in- Pseudo-INF, -um- Pseudo-INF), or orthographically related (Orth.Con). The Prime Type variable controls the relatedness between the prime and the target, which can be related (morphologically, pseudo-morphologically, or orthographically) or completely unrelated.

We also added filler items, which do not form part of the main analysis.", "Participants’ Reaction Time (RT) to the target when preceded by related and unrelated primes will be compared in this study (see Analysis Plan). Participants’ lexical decision accuracy on each trial will determine whether that trial is included or excluded, and participant accuracy rates will determine whether a participant is included or excluded (see Exclusion Criteria).", "We will use Mixed-Effects regression analyses in the lme4 package in R. The model will have Reaction Time (RT) as the dependent variable and RelationType (-in- INF, -um- INF, ni- PREF, ʔ-INF, -in- Pseudo-INF, -um- Pseudo-INF, Orth.Con) crossed with PrimeType (related, unrelated) as fixed effects. The baseline levels for the two fixed factors will be ‘-in- INF’ and ‘unrelated’, respectively. By-subject and by-item random slopes and intercepts will be included as random effects. The initial full model will be coded as: TagPrime ← lmer(RT ~ RelationType * PrimeType + (RelationType*PrimeType|Subject) + (RelationType*PrimeType|Item), REML = F). To choose the best random effects structure, Log-likelihood ratio testing will be used. We will compare models with by-subject and by-item random slopes to the model with only a by-subject random slope. If the less complicated model is more parsimonious based on BIC and AIC, then we will simplify the model by dropping the random slope for items. The same process will be applied to by-subject random slope.

The full model with RelationType * PrimeType interaction will be compared to the model without interaction RelationType + PrimeType. If the less complex model has better goodness of fit, the model will be further simplified by removing RelationType as a factor and compared to the model with this factor. Since the critical criterion for assessing whether we get masked priming effects is obtaining significant priming in -in- INF, -um- INF, ni- PREF, and ʔ-INF (potentially -in- Pseudo-INF, -um- Pseudo-INF), but no significant Orth.Con priming, the RelationType is the most important factor. If RelationType does not make a significant contribution to the model’s goodness of fit, we will consider that we have failed to find the effect.

We will also run separate analyses where the -in- Pseudo-INF and -um- Pseudo-INF conditions will be collapsed into one condition Pseudo-INF to further investigate the decomposition of pseudo-infixed words.

Multiple comparison corrections will be done using the emmeans package in R, particularly Tukey HSD, which will be coded as: TagPrime.emm = emmans(TagPrime, ~ RelationType * PrimeType), then pairs(TagPrime.emm, simple = “each”). This will generate simple main-effect contrast sets, comparing the magnitude of RelationType * PrimeType interaction effects across conditions.", "We will be using the T value >|2| criteria to evaluate significance in our linear mixed models. We are also expecting an effect size of > 20ms for the -in- INF, -um- INF, ni PREF, and ʔ-INF priming effect, which is the effect size commonly reported in masked affix priming literature (see Crepaldi et al., 2015).", "Prior to data analysis, participant error rates for the grammatical items will be calculated. Participants rejecting more than 20% of the real word items will be excluded from analysis. Participants who don’t list Tagalog as of their native language, and who attended primary and secondary school outside of the Philippines will be removed.

Only accurate response data will be included in the RT analyses. We will first remove responses shorter than 200 ms. Further outlier removal will be performed following Baayen and Millin (2010), by fitting a simple mixed model with only random effects and excluding all data points with residuals exceeding 2.5 SD.", "The lmer function in R removes the missing data.", "M. #### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 264 columns across 14 data files.
#### Issues Identified

26 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 14 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Seventy participants with a mean age of 31.27 (SD = 9.764; Range = 19-51) were recruited for the experiment via Prolific.co.
All participants were native speakers of Tagalog, as self-reported in the language background questionnaire.
All participants gave their informed consent, and they were remunerated £3.13 for a 25-minute experiment.
Participants had 2500ms to judge whether the target word was a real Tagalog word or not by pressing the corresponding arrow key (see Figure 1B).
Participants were instructed to respond as quickly and as accurately as possible.
The participants were probed about their perception of the primes.
Participants were asked to report the other languages they speak and whether they took Tagalog classes during their primary and secondary education.
Sixty participants were retained for further cleaning and analyses after the above exclusion.

All participants were native speakers of Tagalog, through self-report.
All participants gave their informed consent, and they were remunerated £3.13 for a 30-minute experiment.

In many of the world's languages, words are built by combining smaller meaningful units called morphemes.
For example, the word mistrustfulness has 4 morphemes: mis-, trust, -ful-, -ness.

Many psycholinguistic models propose that visual recognition of morphologically complex words occurs through the decomposition of such words into morphological units (e.g., Taft & Forster, 1975; Rastle & Davis, 2008; Stockall & Marantz, 2006), such that words like teacher are segmented into {teach}+{-er}.
text.formatted: Many psycholinguistic models propose that visual recognition of morphologically complex words occurs through the decomposition of such words into morphological units (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Taft & Forster, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Rastle & Davis, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Stockall & Marantz, 2006)</ref>, such that words like teacher are segmented into {teach}+{-er}.

text.text: The overwhelming majority of evidence concerning this comes from masked priming (Forster, 1998; Forster & Davis, 1984; Forster et al., 1990).
text.formatted: The overwhelming majority of evidence concerning this comes from masked priming <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Forster, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Forster & Davis, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Forster et al., 1990)</ref>.

text.text: In terms of affixes, it has been shown that recognition of an affixal morpheme in the target (e.g.

TEACHER) is significantly facilitated by a brief presentation of a morphologically related prime sharing the same affix (e.g., builder), as compared to when the target is preceded by a completely unrelated prime (e.g., scandal) (e.g., Chateau et al., 2002; Giraudo and Grainger, 2003; Duñabeitia et al., 2008; Crepaldi et al., 2015; see also Gaston et al. 2023 for long lag and immediate, non-masked affix priming evidence).
text.formatted: TEACHER) is significantly facilitated by a brief presentation of a morphologically related prime sharing the same affix (e.g., builder), as compared to when the target is preceded by a completely unrelated prime (e.g., scandal) (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Chateau et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Giraudo and Grainger, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Duñabeitia et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Crepaldi et al., 2015</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr">Gaston et al. 2023</ref> for long lag and immediate, non-masked affix priming evidence).

text.text: These findings suggest that the representations of affixes are activated after morphologically complex words are segmented. Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023) Word and Affix model proposed that such activation of affixes is constrained by positional information-that is, affixes can only be activated if they are at the edge of the letter-strings, as it makes them salient and highly visible, and if they occur in their canonical position (i.e., after the stem for suffixes, before the stem for prefixes).
text.formatted: These findings suggest that the representations of affixes are activated after morphologically complex words are segmented. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023)</ref> Word and Affix model proposed that such activation of affixes is constrained by positional information-that is, affixes can only be activated if they are at the edge of the letter-strings, as it makes them salient and highly visible, and if they occur in their canonical position (i.e., after the stem for suffixes, before the stem for prefixes).

text.text: However, this constraint may be a product of a narrow evidence base: Cayado and Rastle (2025) found that over 50% of the studies on morphological processing were conducted in suffixation in Indo-European languages over the past 50 years (see also Share 2008 and Frost 2012 on Anglocentricity in reading research), thus it is unclear whether edge-alignment and canonical position are key factors in a wider range of languages.
text.formatted: However, this constraint may be a product of a narrow evidence base: <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cayado and Rastle (2025)</ref> found that over 50% of the studies on morphological processing were conducted in suffixation in Indo-European languages over the past 50 years (see also <ref type="bibr">Share 2008 and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Frost 2012 on</ref> Anglocentricity in reading research), thus it is unclear whether edge-alignment and canonical position are key factors in a wider range of languages.

text.text: In this study, we address this problem by examining how positional information affects affix activation using an understudied morphological phenomenon: Tagalog infixation.
Because infixes occur within the stem and can occupy multiple positions, they provide a critical test-case as to whether edgealignment, canonical position, or both constrain affix activation.
How important are edge-alignment and canonical position in morphological processing?
Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023) Word and Affix Model proposes that affix processing depends on positional information.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023)</ref> Word and Affix Model proposes that affix processing depends on positional information.

text.text: Specifically, they argue that affixes can only be activated [1] if they appear in their canonical position based on their positional encoding (i.e., stringfinal for suffixes, string-initial for prefixes) and [2] if they are edge-aligned.
text.formatted: Specifically, they argue that affixes can only be activated <ref type="bibr">[1]</ref> if they appear in their canonical position based on their positional encoding (i.e., stringfinal for suffixes, string-initial for prefixes) and <ref type="bibr">[2]</ref> if they are edge-aligned.

text.text: Specifically, this model implements affix representations that are encoded with position-specific "boundness" in the lexicon.

For instance, prefixes are encoded as un_ and re_, with underscore lines indicating that letter strings can only be placed to the right, while suffixes are encoded as _ity and _er, with underscore lines indicating that letter strings can only be placed to the left.
The claim that position relative to a stem is a key part of affix representation is not exactly new.

For example, Chomsky and Halle (1968) in the Sound Pattern of English, as well as Taft and Forster (1975, 1976) in the Affix Stripping Model annotate prefixes and suffixes with + encode positional information.
text.formatted: For example, Chomsky and <ref type="bibr">Halle (1968)</ref> in the Sound Pattern of English, as well as <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Taft and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Forster (1975, 1976)</ref> in the Affix Stripping Model annotate prefixes and suffixes with + encode positional information.

text.text: But Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023) model claims that both canonical position and edge-alignment are critical to affix activation and recognition.
text.formatted: But <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023)</ref> model claims that both canonical position and edge-alignment are critical to affix activation and recognition.

text.text: Some key evidence for the importance of positional encoding comes from Crepaldi et al. (2016).
text.formatted: Some key evidence for the importance of positional encoding comes from <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Crepaldi et al. (2016)</ref>.

text.text: In a pair of masked priming experiments, they showed that affix processing in English depends on positional information encoding.

Specifically, responses to the target affix -er are only significantly facilitated by a morphologically structured nonword like sheeter, where 'er' appears in its canonical position, but not in ersheet, where it appears in a noncanonical position.

This is in contrast to stem activation, which has been shown to occur in a position-independent manner, such that the stem pay in payment is activated when preceded by a suffixed prime payable or a prefixed prime prepay (Feldman & Larabee, 2001; see also Crepaldi et al. 2013 for masked transposed priming evidence).
text.formatted: This is in contrast to stem activation, which has been shown to occur in a position-independent manner, such that the stem pay in payment is activated when preceded by a suffixed prime payable or a prefixed prime prepay <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Feldman & Larabee, 2001</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Crepaldi et al. 2013</ref> for masked transposed priming evidence).

text.text: This reflects the fact that stems naturally appear in different linear positions (e.g., dress in dresser vs. overdress).

In 2016, Crepaldi et al. noted that none of the existing psycholinguistic models made explicit claims about how positional information is encoded in a way that allows position-specific (affixes) and position-free (stems) representations within the system. Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023) word and affix model is the first to make this explicit formulation, which motivates further investigation of the phenomena. Spencer et al. (2024) further corroborated the idea of position-specific affix processing by comparing processing of stems, prefixes, and suffixes in English.
text.formatted: In 2016, <ref type="bibr">Crepaldi et al.</ref> noted that none of the existing psycholinguistic models made explicit claims about how positional information is encoded in a way that allows position-specific (affixes) and position-free (stems) representations within the system. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023)</ref> word and affix model is the first to make this explicit formulation, which motivates further investigation of the phenomena. <ref type="bibr">Spencer et al. (2024)</ref> further corroborated the idea of position-specific affix processing by comparing processing of stems, prefixes, and suffixes in English.

text.text: They revealed that transposed compound words were harder to reject than their controls (e.g., dreamday vs. shadeday), whereas there was no difference between transposed suffixed words and their controls (e.g., fulpain vs. adepain), or between transposed prefixed words and their controls (e.g., qualifydis vs. qualifymis).
These findings further suggest that affixes are only successfully activated when they appear in their canonical position.

However, the empirical evidence that affix activation is dependent on the affix appearing in its canonical position comes from studies that displace those affixes to the opposite position (e.g., suffixes in prefix position and vice versa) where they not only violate positional encoding but also create nonwords (e.g., ersheet, qualifydis).
Further, these studies have only looked at prefixes and suffixes in Indo-European languages.

The assumption that affix activation is constrained by edge-alignment and strict positional information only works for words that only contain one stem and one prefix or suffix (see Korochkina and Rastle, 2025 for the distribution of complex words with only one stem and affix vs. complex words with multiple affixes). Spencer et al. (2025) examined cases where suffixes are stacked next to each other and found that English suffixes like -ness and -er can be activated even when they are embedded in the middle of letter strings, as in the case of the nonwords spitenessful (derived from spitefulness) and bestersell (derived from bestseller).
text.formatted: The assumption that affix activation is constrained by edge-alignment and strict positional information only works for words that only contain one stem and one prefix or suffix (see Korochkina and Rastle, 2025 for the distribution of complex words with only one stem and affix vs. complex words with multiple affixes). <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Spencer et al. (2025)</ref> examined cases where suffixes are stacked next to each other and found that English suffixes like -ness and -er can be activated even when they are embedded in the middle of letter strings, as in the case of the nonwords spitenessful (derived from spitefulness) and bestersell (derived from bestseller).

text.text: These findings suggest that, provided their canonical position relative to the stem (left or right) is preserved, English suffixes can be activated even when they are not edge-aligned or occur in their expected order relative to other affixes (e.g., spitenessful).
In other words, this study shows that canonical position relative to the stem is necessary, but edge-alignment is not.

However, Spencer et al. (2025) examined only nonword processing and English suffixation, and they did not investigate whether such positional flexibility is evident during the earliest stages of visual word-form processing, since they did not utilise any subliminal prime presentation.
text.formatted: However, <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Spencer et al. (2025)</ref> examined only nonword processing and English suffixation, and they did not investigate whether such positional flexibility is evident during the earliest stages of visual word-form processing, since they did not utilise any subliminal prime presentation.

text.text: Thus, crosslinguistic evidence for flexible affix activation remains very limited, and it is unclear whether the flexibility identified by Spencer et al. extends to early morphoorthographic processing. Crepaldi et al. (2016) noted that positional constraints arise from the distributional properties of morphemes within the language: suffixes were not identified when they occur at the beginning of letter-strings because never occur in this position in the real language, while prefixes were not identified at the end of letter-strings because they likewise never occur in this position.
text.formatted: Thus, crosslinguistic evidence for flexible affix activation remains very limited, and it is unclear whether the flexibility identified by Spencer et al. extends to early morphoorthographic processing. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Crepaldi et al. (2016)</ref> noted that positional constraints arise from the distributional properties of morphemes within the language: suffixes were not identified when they occur at the beginning of letter-strings because never occur in this position in the real language, while prefixes were not identified at the end of letter-strings because they likewise never occur in this position.

text.text: On this view, positional constraints reflect the statistical regularities of the linguistic input within the word identification system, which can vary across languages.

By looking at Tagalog infixation, the present study can tease apart the importance of edge-alignment and canonical position as established by distributional regularities without relying on nonword processing.

Thus, these findings show that morphological decomposition occurs in the absence of stem or affix edge-alignment when the distributional regularities of morphemes in the language support it.
Note that Cayado et al. (2023) only show that stems in infixed words can be successfully activated despite being discontinuous and not edge-aligned.

text.text: It therefore remains unclear whether canonical position or edge-alignment affect the detection and activation of affixes in the earliest stage of visual word recognition.

We address this issue in the present study using masked affix priming, where affixes are presented subliminally in the prime, and by looking at Tagalog infixation, where affixes are inserted within the stem and can occur in multiple positions relative to the stem.
We exploit Tagalog infixation and pseudo-infixation to address the issue outlined above.
Tagalog has two inflectional infixes, namely <um> which marks agent voice and <in> which marks perfective aspect.
text.formatted: Tagalog has two inflectional infixes, namely <um> which marks agent voice and <in> which marks perfective aspect.

text.text: Both of these infixes are typically inserted after a consonant but before the first vowel in a letter string (1a).
Further, <in> and <um> can orthographically appear in the left-edge position when attached to glottal stop-initial stems, due to /ʔ/ being unwritten in Tagalog (1b).

text.text: In this case, both infixes are phonologically infixes but orthographically at the beginning of the letter-string, which is a non-canonical position for infixes.

text.text: These infixes, and their varying linear positioning, provide an important test-case to examine the extent to which early decomposition relies on edge-alignment.

In the present study, we compare the processing of <in> and <um> when they occur in the canonical infix position [that is, after the first consonant in the stem, see (1a)] and when they are in the non-canonical, left-edge position [that is, the beginning of the word, see (1b)] using masked affix priming to see whether edge-alignment and canonical position offer some advantage during the early stage of visual recognition of affixes.

text.text: It has been shown in the previous literature examining English that stem variants prime each other.

For example, studies have found robust masked priming effects for irregularly inflected words like sang-SING and fell-FALL (Crepaldi et al., 2010; Morris & Stockall, 2012; Fruchter et al., 2013), suggesting that the brief presentation of an irregularly inflected prime like fell is sufficient to activate the stem variant fall and the abstract [+past] morpheme after segmentation, which then facilitates the recognition of the stem variant when it is encountered as the target [see Fruchter et al. text.text: This proposed process also makes the decomposition of pseudo-infixed words possible, since it aligns with the [1] case, where the -in-or -um-bigram is preceded by a consonant.
The present study aims to further test this proposal by using masked affix priming, a paradigm that specifically examines affix activation during decomposition.

So far, masked affix priming effects have been attested in prefixation in English (e.g., irrelevant-IRRATIONAL, Chateau et al., 2002), Spanish (e.g., incapaz-INFELIZ, Dominguez et al., 2010), and French (e.g., enjeu-ENVOL, Giraudo & Grainger, 2003).

text.text: For suffixation, reliable masked affix priming effects have only been demonstrated in English (Duñabeitia et al., 2008; Crepaldi et al., 2015).

text.text: Evidently, the existing studies on affix activation have mainly focused on prefixation and suffixation in Indo-European languages, where affixes are placed at the edges of the words, making this activation more straightforward due to the high visibility of the affixes.

It is yet to be investigated whether infixes are successfully activated after morphological segmentation in the same way that prefixes and suffixes are (but see Cayado et al., 2023 for stem priming with infixed words).

text.text: The investigation of infixation in the masked affix priming literature is crucial as it allows the examination of whether rapid affix detection and activation is constrained by strict edge-alignment or whether it is shaped by languagespecific distributional regularities of affixes in the language.

We conducted two experiments to investigate whether orthographic left edge-alignment or canonical affix position facilitate rapid affix detection and activation under masked priming conditions, where visual exposure to the prime is minimal.
Previous experiments have been unable to disentangle the influence of edge-alignment and distributional properties since these two factors were confounded by their reliance on nonword processing.

Tagalog infixation provides a critical test because these factors make contrasting predictions: if edges are indeed privileged due to their salience, as proposed by Beyersmann and Grainger (2023), then the left edge-aligned infixes (e.g., inayos 'fixed') should be detected and activated more easily and rapidly than internal infixes (e.g., tinawag 'called').
text.formatted: Tagalog infixation provides a critical test because these factors make contrasting predictions: if edges are indeed privileged due to their salience, as proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Beyersmann and Grainger (2023)</ref>, then the left edge-aligned infixes (e.g., inayos 'fixed') should be detected and activated more easily and rapidly than internal infixes (e.g., tinawag 'called').

text.text: In contrast, if affix detection and activation mechanisms are shaped by language-specific distributional factors, perhaps encoded as positional constraints as proposed by Crepaldi et al. (2016) and Beyersmann and Grainger (2023), then <in> and <um> infixes should be detected and activated more efficiently when they occur in their canonical position (i.e., between the first consonant and the first vowel) than when they occur in the non-canonical position at the left edge.

(2016)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Beyersmann and Grainger (2023)</ref>, then <in> and <um> infixes should be detected and activated more efficiently when they occur in their canonical position (i.e., between the first consonant and the first vowel) than when they occur in the non-canonical position at the left edge.

text.text: If edge-alignment offers an advantage in affix detection and activation, as proposed by Beyersmann and Grainger (2023), then robust priming effects should be obtained when the primes have an <in> infix in the left-edge position and the targets have <in> infix in the canonical position but not for the opposite combination.

text.text: However, if edge-alignment does not offer any advantage, then robust priming effects should also be obtained when the primes have an <in> infix in the canonical position and the targets have an <in> infix in the left-edge position.

Additionally, if affix variants are activated after segmentation in the same way that stem variants are, then priming effects should be observed for word pairs sharing <in>/ni-variants.

text.text: Seventy participants with a mean age of 31.27 (SD = 9.764; Range = 19-51) were recruited for the experiment via Prolific.co.
All participants were native speakers of Tagalog, as self-reported in the language background questionnaire.
We asked them about their city of origin in the Philippines and checked whether Tagalog is the dominant language in that area.
All participants also reported speaking English.
Others additionally spoke another Philippine language (N=16), Italian (N=3), Spanish (N=1), Swedish (N=1), and Japanese (N=1).
All participants reported doing their primary and secondary education in the Philippines.
The experiment was overseen by the first author's university human subjects' ethics review board.
All participants gave their informed consent, and they were remunerated £3.13 for a 25-minute experiment.

text.text: This set included both real morphologically complex words and pseudoinfixed words.
As a second step, we coded these items as complex or simple based on the linguistic judgements of the first author, who is a native Tagalog speaker.
These linguistic judgements were further confirmed by checking if the ones tagged as morphologically complex have the same meaning in the dictionary as other words sharing the same stem.

These items were then further checked based on the phonological environment: a real infix is typically followed by a vowel (e.g., tinawag), while a pseudo-infix is typically followed by another consonant (e.g., kintab).
This test was able to effectively exclude pseudo-infixed words, but the remaining complex word list also contained items that may have been fossilized.
For example, the word t<in>apay is historically an infixed word meaning 'the process of making bread' but is now used as a monomorphemic word meaning 'bread'.

text.text: Additionally, there was also an orthographic control (ORTHCON) condition with 40 trials (20 related, 20 unrelated).

This orthographic control condition consisted of monomorphemic prime-target words with an orthographic overlap in the first three letters (lampin-LAMBAT 'diaper-NET', bunyag-BUNDOL 'reveal-HIT LIGHTLY').

These monomorphemic target words were also preceded by unrelated primes, which are words that have no overlap in the first three letters with the target (e.g., bughaw-LAMBAT 'blue-NET', pigtas-BUNDOL 'break off-HIT LIGHTLY').
The first three-letter overlap was chosen in this condition because the orthographic overlap in the critical conditions is also in that position.
The items and their lexical frequencies were extracted using SketchEngine.
Only words that were 4-8 letters long with lexical frequency of above 0.05 per million were retained from the candidate set.

text.text: Since all participants saw the critical targets in both their related prime and unrelated prime condition, we ensured that the two occurrences of each target were separated into two different blocks, with a short break in between to minimize possible long distance priming effects.

The order of items within a block was pseudo-randomized for each participant, and the order of the two blocks was permuted across participants such that each block occurred as the first block for half of the participants and as the second block for the other half.
The task started with a consent form, followed by a brief instruction and a practice session of 10 trials.
All visual stimuli were presented in the center of the screen, in black 50point size Courier Sans Serif over a white background to provide a contrast.

Each trial began with a fixation cross for 500ms, followed by a 500ms presentation of a forward mask made up of a row of hash marks (e.g., ########), matching the maximum length of the corresponding prime.
Immediately afterward, the prime was displayed for 33ms in lowercase letters, followed by the target in uppercase letters.
Participants had 2500ms to judge whether the target word was a real Tagalog word or not by pressing the corresponding arrow key (see Figure 1B).
text.formatted: Participants had 2500ms to judge whether the target word was a real Tagalog word or not by pressing the corresponding arrow key (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1B</ref>).

text.text: We also controlled the mapping of 'Yes' and 'No' to the arrow keys, to ensure results were not dependent on this mapping.
For half of the participants, Oo (Tagalog: 'Yes') mapped to the left arrow key and Hindi (Tagalog: 'No') mapped to the right arrow key, while the other half experienced the opposite mapping.
Participants were instructed to respond as quickly and as accurately as possible.
The entire experiment took thirty minutes to finish.
The participants were probed about their perception of the primes.
No participants reported having noticed the masked primes.

There are two possibilities that may explain these differential findings.

On the one hand, it is possible that seeing a left edge-aligned affix in the prime offers some advantage during affix detection and the subsequent activation of an affix representation, which leads to significant priming effects for the GLOTTAL-INF/IN-INF condition, but not vice versa.
On the other hand, it might be the case that edge-alignment only offers some advantage during affix activation if there is an alignment mismatch in the affixes in the prime and the target.
Perhaps, edge-alignment in the prime may resolve any difficulty caused by mismatched orthographic positions of affixes in primes and targets.
Experiment 2 further explores these two possibilities.

Finally, no robust priming effects were observed for the GLOTTAL-INF/NI-PREF (e.g., conditions, but a non-significant 13ms facilitation was found for the former, where the prime has <in> in the left-edge position and the target is a ni-prefixed word.

text.text: Another explanation can be derived from a transformational model of morphology like Distributed Morphology (Halle & Marantz, 1993; Embick, 2015), where the ni-prefix variant has been proposed to be the default case, while the <in> infix variant is the result of phonological readjustment, particularly onset metathesis (see Halle, 2001).

text.text: It is, therefore, possible that the 33ms presentation of the prime is not enough time for participants to unpack the phonological readjustment mapping <in> to ni-, thereby preventing any priming boost for the ni-prefix in target words.

text.text: In other words, activating a phonological variant in the mental lexicon after segmentation may take more time.
This latter possibility is further investigated in Experiment 2.

In this experiment, we showed that the <in> infix is successfully activated [1] when it appears in the left-edge-position in both prime and target words (SAMEPOS), and [2] when it appears after a consonant in the target word after being preceded by a prime word where <in> is in the left-edge position (GLOTTAL-INF/IN-INF).
text.formatted: In this experiment, we showed that the <in> infix is successfully activated [1] when it appears in the left-edge-position in both prime and target words (SAMEPOS), and [2] when it appears after a consonant in the target word after being preceded by a prime word where <in> is in the left-edge position (GLOTTAL-INF/IN-INF).

text.text: However, we have also shown that the variation of affix form and position modulates priming effects, as the priming boost disappeared in all other critical conditions, which may be attributed to phonological readjustments, edge-alignment, or positional mismatch.
In Experiment 2, we investigate these possibilities by keeping the form and position of affixes constant between prime and target.
Additionally, we also test whether the influence of edge-alignment applies to both real infixes and pseudo-infixes, which are monomorphemic words with -in-and -um-bigrams after a consonant.

In this experiment, we aim to further investigate the effects of edge-alignment and canonical affix positions using word pairs where affixes are in the same orthographic linear position in primes and targets.

If infixes in the canonical position are not successfully detected due to not being edge-aligned, as suggested in Experiment 1, then no reliable priming effects should be obtained for word pairs sharing the same <in> and <um> infixes in the canonical within-stem position.
text.formatted: If infixes in the canonical position are not successfully detected due to not being edge-aligned, as suggested in Experiment 1, then no reliable priming effects should be obtained for word pairs sharing the same <in> and <um> infixes in the canonical within-stem position.

text.text: However, if edge-alignment does not offer some advantage during affix activation, then similar priming should be observed for word pairs sharing affixes in the left-edge position (e.g., inayos 'fixed', umalis 'left', ninakaw 'stole') and word pairs sharing infixes after a consonant (e.g., tinawag 'called', sumayaw 'to dance').
These findings would support the idea that neither edge-alignment nor canonical position are critical for affix activation.

Finally, if edge-alignment operates based on morpho-orthographic forms, then monomorphemic word pairs sharing -in-and -um-bigrams in canonical infix positions should exhibit priming effects in pseudo-infixed conditions.

text.text: Eighty participants with a mean age of 32.06 (SD = 9.402; Range = 20-57) were recruited for the experiment via Prolific. co.

All participants also reported speaking English.

All participants gave their informed consent, and they were remunerated £3.13 for a 30-minute experiment.

There were four critical conditions in this experiment containing real morphologically complex words, with 40 trials each (20 related, 20 unrelated ): [1] the <in> infix (INF) condition, where the prime and target share the same <in> infix; [2] the <um> infix (INF) condition, where the prime and the target share the <um> infix; [3] the ni-prefix (PREF) condition, where the prime and the target share the same ni-prefix; and [4] the glottal infix (GLOTTAL-INF) condition, in which the prime and target both had the <in> infix attached to a glottal stop initial stem.

Further, we also found significant priming effects for the <IN> INF and <UM> INF conditions, suggesting that infixes in their canonical position are successfully detected and activated even when they are not edge-aligned in either the prime or target.

text.text: Significant priming effects also emerged for the PSEUDO-INF condition where the -in-and -um-bigrams are collapsed into one condition, but not for either pseudoinfix condition separately.
The priming effects observed in this study must be morphological in nature, as we did not find reliable priming effects for the orthographic control condition.
These results suggest that the <in> and <um> (pseudo)infixes, as well as <in> when it orthographically appears in the left-edge position, are successfully activated after segmentation.

text.text: Findings from this experiment provide compelling evidence that affixes can be detected and their representations subsequently activated, regardless of edge-alignment and canonical position.
Our results extend the findings of Cayado et al. (2023) that stems can be activated despite being outer-embedded.
text.formatted: Our results extend the findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cayado et al. (2023)</ref> that stems can be activated despite being outer-embedded.

text.text: We also show that neither edge-alignment nor canonical position affect the initial stage of visual word recognition, thereby extending the English data from Spencer et al. (2025), which used morpheme interference paradigm.
text.formatted: We also show that neither edge-alignment nor canonical position affect the initial stage of visual word recognition, thereby extending the English data from <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Spencer et al. (2025)</ref>, which used morpheme interference paradigm.

text.text: Further, the finding that pseudo-infixed primes may have reliably primed pseudo-infixed targets when the two conditions are collapsed is particularly unexpected if edge-alignment were required for affix detection or activation, since the -in-and -um-strings are not even functioning as real infixes in these words.
But we acknowledge that this effect is only reliable when the two pseudoinfixed conditions are collapsed into one condition, suggesting that this effect might be weaker.
This is consistent with the findings of Wray et al. (2022).
text.formatted: This is consistent with the findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Wray et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: These findings are therefore difficult to reconcile with a model (Beyersmann & Grainger, 2023) in which edge-alignment and canonical position are necessary for affix activation.
text.formatted: These findings are therefore difficult to reconcile with a model <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Beyersmann & Grainger, 2023)</ref> in which edge-alignment and canonical position are necessary for affix activation.

text.text: Finally, no reliable priming effects were observed for the NI-PREF condition.
This makes it unlikely that the lack of priming from <in> to ni-in Experiment 1 was solely due to extra processing required to relate the <in> and ni-variants (e.g., phonological readjustment).

text.text: Here, we find no significant priming from ni-to ni-, suggesting that the ni-prefix is not consistently detected/segmented in the prime.

This may be due to three possible reasons: first, the ni-variant is much less frequent than the <in> infix variant; second, it occurs in a very restricted set of phonological environments (and thus orthographic environments); and third, it typically exhibits optionality in its occurrence [that is, ni-hiwa and h<in>iwa 'sliced' are both possible options].

text.text: These factors are not mutually exclusive, and all or some combination of these factors may either reduce the probability of parsing the string ni-as a morpheme at all, or reduce the probability of rapidly activating a representation of the affix sufficiently to boost priming.
However, Cayado et al. (2023) showed evidence that ni-prefixed words are indeed decomposed into morphemes using the masked stem priming paradigm.

text.text: It is, therefore, not the case that ni-prefixed words are not decomposed at all.
It is, then, more likely that it is only the subsequent re-activation of the affix representation that was less robust for ni-than for <in>.
