text.text: The main goal of the present study is to test whether orthographic left edge-alignment or canonical affix position facilitate rapid affix detection and activation during morphoorthographic processing.
We conducted two visual masked affix priming experiments to investigate this question, using infixation in Tagalog as a test-case.
In Experiment 1, we found robust priming effects for both SAME-POS (e.g., inamoy-INIPIT 'smelled-STUCK') and GLOTTAL-INF/IN-INF (e.g., inahit-TINAHI 'shaved-STITCHED') conditions.

This shows that the <in> infix can be successfully activated after segmentation when it appears in the noncanonical, left-edge position in both prime and target words, and when it appears left edge aligned in the prime, but after a consonant in the target word.
text.formatted: This shows that the <in> infix can be successfully activated after segmentation when it appears in the noncanonical, left-edge position in both prime and target words, and when it appears left edge aligned in the prime, but after a consonant in the target word.

text.text: In Experiment 2, we observed robust priming effects for <in>INF, <um>INF, and GLOTTAL-INF conditions, as well as the PSEUDO-INF condition, but only when -in-and -um-are collapsed into one condition.
text.formatted: In Experiment 2, we observed robust priming effects for <in>INF, <um>INF, and GLOTTAL-INF conditions, as well as the PSEUDO-INF condition, but only when -in-and -um-are collapsed into one condition.

text.text: Together with Wray et al.'s (2022) MEG results, findings from this experiment suggest that both real infixes and pseudo-infixes are activated during the initial stage of visual word recognition.

The present study extends the ontological breadth of the current masked affix priming literature, which has mainly focused on prefixation and suffixation (e.g., Chateau et al., 2002; Dominguez et al., 2010; Giraudo & Grainger, 2003; Crepaldi et al., 2015; Duñabeitia et al., 2008).
text.formatted: The present study extends the ontological breadth of the current masked affix priming literature, which has mainly focused on prefixation and suffixation (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Chateau et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Dominguez et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Giraudo & Grainger, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Crepaldi et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Duñabeitia et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: By doing so, we provide psycholinguistic data that shows a more nuanced influence of positional information on affix activation.
Specifically, findings from the present study ultimately show that edge-alignment and canonical position are not critical factors for affix activation.

In Experiment 1, the noncanonical, left-edge-aligned <in> infix is activated after segmentation of the prime, leading to faster processing the <in> infix in the target when it appears in the canonical condition This encoding aligns with the findings of Crepaldi et al. (2016), where the English suffix -er is only activated when it appears in its canonical position (e.g., sheeter) but not when it appears in a non-canonical position (ersheet).

(2016)</ref>, where the English suffix -er is only activated when it appears in its canonical position (e.g., sheeter) but not when it appears in a non-canonical position (ersheet).

text.text: However, this study placed suffixes in a position where they do not ever appear (i.e., before their stem).

In the case of Tagalog, we found that <in> in the left-edge orthographic position (e.g., in-ayos 'fixed') significantly facilitated <in> when it is preceded by a consonant (e.g., t<in>awag 'called'), suggesting that affix activation takes place in at least two positions, which may be due to a more flexible positional information encoding of <in>, due to the distributional properties of affixes in Tagalog.

text.text: These findings are consistent with Spencer et al. (2025), where they showed that the English suffix -ness is recognised in two different positions, as long as both positions are after a stem (e.g., spitefulness vs. spitenessful). Crepaldi et al. (2016) proposed that positional constraints arise from morpheme distribution within the language.

(2016)</ref> proposed that positional constraints arise from morpheme distribution within the language.

text.text: It is therefore possible that skilled, adult readers of Tagalog are able to strip the <in> and <um> infixes very rapidly because they have been sufficiently exposed to the distributional properties of these infixes in the writing system (that is, the #C_ context in which they consistently appear), making a word initial consonant a reliable cue to infixation.
text.formatted: It is therefore possible that skilled, adult readers of Tagalog are able to strip the <in> and <um> infixes very rapidly because they have been sufficiently exposed to the distributional properties of these infixes in the writing system (that is, the #C_ context in which they consistently appear), making a word initial consonant a reliable cue to infixation.

text.text: Exposure to the different positions in which affixes occur seems to have helped develop implicit knowledge of the positional distribution of these affixes, which then allows decomposition to take place, regardless of edge-alignment.

Perhaps, in Tagalog, <in> is tagged as _in_/in_ in its form representation which would allow activation of the affix when it appears in the non-canonical left-edge position (e.g., inayos 'fixed') or when it is preceded by a consonant (e.g., tinawag 'called').
text.formatted: Perhaps, in Tagalog, <in> is tagged as _in_/in_ in its form representation which would allow activation of the affix when it appears in the non-canonical left-edge position (e.g., inayos 'fixed') or when it is preceded by a consonant (e.g., tinawag 'called').

text.text: Overall, our results are consistent with previous experimental work on Tagalog infixed and circumfixed words (Cayado et al., 2023; Wray et al., 2022), English words where suffixes are stacked next to each other (e.g., spitenessful, see Spencer et al., 2025), as well as work on Semitic languages, where complex words are decomposed into morphological pieces, even though these morphemes are not edge-aligned (e.g., Frost et al., 1997 Frost et al., , 2000;; Boudelaa & Marslen-Wilson 2005 , 2011; Kastner et al., 2018).

text.text: The present study, therefore, prompts necessary revision to theories of morphological processing that require strict edge-alignment and canonical position (Beyersmann & Grainger, 2023) to accommodate this new data.

text.text: Experiment 1 also tested whether affix variants are activated after segmentation.

We did not find significant priming effects for word pairs containing the <in> infix (whether it is in the left-edge position or after a consonant) as a prime and the ni-prefix as a target, despite these affixes being variants of the same morpheme.
text.formatted: We did not find significant priming effects for word pairs containing the <in> infix (whether it is in the left-edge position or after a consonant) as a prime and the ni-prefix as a target, despite these affixes being variants of the same morpheme.

text.text: There are many possibilities as to why we did not get priming effects for these affix variants.

Under transformational models of morphology like Distributed Morphology (Halle & Marantz, 1993; Embick, 2015), infixes are underlyingly prefixes that went through phonological readjustment (Kalin, 2022).
text.formatted: Under transformational models of morphology like Distributed Morphology <ref type="bibr">(Halle & Marantz, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Embick, 2015)</ref>, infixes are underlyingly prefixes that went through phonological readjustment <ref type="bibr">(Kalin, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In the case of Tagalog, the <in> infix is underlyingly the ni-prefix (i.e., the default form) that undergoes phonological readjustment, particularly onset metathesis (Halle, 2001).
text.formatted: In the case of Tagalog, the <in> infix is underlyingly the ni-prefix (i.e., the default form) that undergoes phonological readjustment, particularly onset metathesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Halle, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Activating the mental representation of the ni-from <in>, therefore, would require unpacking this phonological readjustment first, which may take more time.

text.text: The 33 ms prime presentation in masked priming paradigm may not be enough time to unpack the phonological operation that enables the activation of the representation of ni-from <in>.

text.text: Alternatively, it may also be the case that the infix <in> did activate its variant ni-, but the high form overlap between the two variants might have caused some competition, thereby cancelling out any potential initial facilitation for affix variants.

text.text: In contrast, robust priming effects have been observed for stem variants.

For example, in irregular past tense verbs in English, robust masked priming effects have been observed for prime-target pairs like taught-TEACH and gave-GIVE (e.g., Crepaldi et al., 2010; Morris & Stockall, 2012; Fruchter et al., 2013).
text.formatted: For example, in irregular past tense verbs in English, robust masked priming effects have been observed for prime-target pairs like taught-TEACH and gave-GIVE (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Crepaldi et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Morris & Stockall, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Fruchter et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: One factor that may determine whether one variant would prime another is the reliability of the phonological rule relating the two variants (Fruchter et al., 2013).
text.formatted: One factor that may determine whether one variant would prime another is the reliability of the phonological rule relating the two variants <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Fruchter et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, Fruchter et al. revealed that stem variant pairs like bleed~bled and read~red evoked significant priming in a neural measure (the M170 is reduced for related pairs compared to unrelated pairs), as these variants apply a highly reliable phonological rule [i.e., i → ɛ/ [X {l, r} ___ d][+past]], while no such effects were found for stem variants with less consistent phonological patterns.
Future research should take into account the reliability of the phonological rule that relates affix variants and investigate how this affects affix activation.
The lack of facilitation for ni-may be best explained by how frequently and variably it is used in the language.
The ni-prefix only appears in a limited phonological (and thus orthographic) environment (for l-, w-, y-, h, and n-initial stems), thereby limiting Tagalog speakers' exposure to this prefix.
In fact, it is far less frequent than its <in> infix variant (14,711 per million frequency for <in> vs. 1,382 per million frequency for ni-).
text.formatted: In fact, it is far less frequent than its <in> infix variant (14,711 per million frequency for <in> vs. 1,382 per million frequency for ni-).

text.text: Moreover, the occurrence of the ni-prefix can also exhibit some variability, for example, 'ni-hiwa' and 'h<in>iwa' are both possible options for the word 'sliced'.
text.formatted: Moreover, the occurrence of the ni-prefix can also exhibit some variability, for example, 'ni-hiwa' and 'h<in>iwa' are both possible options for the word 'sliced'.

text.text: The results of Experiment 2 make the phonological readjustment account in Experiment 1 unlikely since no reliable priming effects were found when both primes and targets have the ni-prefix.

It is more likely that the combination of lower frequency, limited phonological environment, and variability could have made it difficult for native Tagalog speakers to activate the ni-prefix, especially in an experimental setting where the prefixed word prime, such as nilumpo 'crippled', was only presented for 33 ms.
This corroborates the idea that the distributional properties of morphemes in the language shape affix activation.
Note that Cayado et al. (2023) showed that ni-prefixed words are nonetheless subject to early decomposition, as evidenced by masked stem priming effects.
text.formatted: Note that <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cayado et al. (2023)</ref> showed that ni-prefixed words are nonetheless subject to early decomposition, as evidenced by masked stem priming effects.

text.text: It might therefore be the case that native Tagalog speakers are able to successfully segment nilumpo 'crippled' into {ni-}+{lumpo}, but the subsequent re-activation of the niaffix representation may have been weaker due to low frequency and variability.
Finally, one challenge in conducting experiments on understudied languages and morphological systems is the limited availability of participants and suitable experimental items.

We acknowledge that the final number of usable datapoints in the present study fell below the recommended threshold of 1,600 observations (Brysbaert & Stevens, 2018) for related and unrelated primes across all conditions in both experiments.
text.formatted: We acknowledge that the final number of usable datapoints in the present study fell below the recommended threshold of 1,600 observations (Brysbaert & Stevens, 2018) for related and unrelated primes across all conditions in both experiments.

text.text: Consequently, the absence of reliable priming effects in some conditions may be attributable to this relatively smaller dataset.
Future work should therefore include a replication study conducted in the Philippines, where access to a larger pool of native speakers would allow for increased statistical power.

In summary, the apparent importance of canonical position and edge-alignment reported in Crepaldi et al. (2016) and related studies, and formalised as key features of Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023) word and affix model, may partly reflect the small typological range of languages from which these accounts have been developed.
text.formatted: In summary, the apparent importance of canonical position and edge-alignment reported in <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Crepaldi et al. (2016)</ref> and related studies, and formalised as key features of <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023)</ref> word and affix model, may partly reflect the small typological range of languages from which these accounts have been developed.

text.text: Much of this research has focused on languages in which affixes occur in a single position relative to the stem, are either left-or right-edge-aligned, and do not interleave with other morphemes.
Neither factor appears to be particularly important in Tagalog, where infixes are canonically interleaved within the stem and appear in multiple positions relative to the stem.
Across our experiments, we instead find evidence for a more flexible encoding of positional information, whereby affixes can be activated in different positions in which they occur in the language.

If Crepaldi et al.'s (2016) proposal is correct that positional constraints emerge from the distributional properties of morphemes within a language, similar flexibility should be expected in languages with 'mobile' affixes like Huave (isolate, Mexico), where the same affix /t/ can appear after the stem as a suffix with a CV cluster (e.g., mohko-t 's/he lay face down') or before the stem as a prefix with VC cluster (e.g., t-uc 's/he ate') [see Zukoff (2021) and Kim (2008 Kim ( , 2010 Kim ( , 2015) ) for a formal analysis].

text.text: The same logic may extend to languages with floating morphemes, such as the floating tones found across a wide range of African languages. Cayado and Rastle (2025) argued that the focus on English and related Indo-European morphology in the past 50 years has led to narrow theorising about morphological processing.
text.formatted: The same logic may extend to languages with floating morphemes, such as the floating tones found across a wide range of African languages. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cayado and Rastle (2025)</ref> argued that the focus on English and related Indo-European morphology in the past 50 years has led to narrow theorising about morphological processing.

text.text: The contribution of the present study extends beyond adding another language to the literature: by examining a morphological system in which the effects of edge-alignment and distributional properties can be directly disentangled, we provide evidence that the positional encoding of morphemes is more flexible than existing models suggest.

To date, Tagalog visual word recognition has only been investigated twice in psycholinguistics (Cayado et al., 2023; 2025) and three times in neurolinguistics (Wray et al., 2022; Cayado et al., 2024; 2025).
text.formatted: To date, Tagalog visual word recognition has only been investigated twice in psycholinguistics <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cayado et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2025)</ref> and three times in neurolinguistics <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Wray et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cayado et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2025)</ref>.

text.text: Further research on understudied languages with unique morphological phenomena is therefore essential for identifying both the systematicities and variation in morphological processing across languages.

text.text: This pattern of results initially suggests that the <in> infix is not rapidly detected when it appears in the canonical position and edge-alignment may be required during the earliest stages of affix detection and activation.However, in Experiment 2, skilled Tagalog readers successfully detected and activated the <in> and <um> infixes (e.g., <in>INF: biniro-SINALO 'joked-CAUGHT'; <um>INF: kumulo-DUMAYO 'to boil-TO VISIT') in the prime despite these elements not being edgealigned, resulting in faster processing of these infixes in the target word.

text.text: The way this detection and activation take place seems to be at a similar level of ease as activating <in> infix in the non-canonical, left-edge-aligned position (i.e., SAME-POS condition).Spencer et al. (2025)</ref> et al. showed that suffixes are activated despite not being edge-aligned, provided that they preserve their canonical position relative to the stem.

text.text: Our findings extend this work by showing that infixes can be activated regardless of edge-alignment and canonical position.The lack of priming in Experiment 1 for the IN-INF/GLOTTAL-INF condition may reflect post-access interference arising from uncertainty during lexical decision when there is a positional mismatch between the prime and target.

Specifically, when the infix occupied its canonical position in the prime but occurred in the non-canonical, left edge-aligned position in the target, no priming advantage emerged, despite the reverse configuration producing priming.

This asymmetry suggests that canonical position may influence processing, but perhaps only at the level of a metalinguistic task such as lexical decision, rather than during the initial automatic form-based detection and activation of the affix.
Another question we explored in this study is how positional information of affixes is encoded in the mental lexicon.
Beyersmann and Grainger's (2023) Word and Affix Model implements affix representations that are encoded with position-specific "boundness" in the orthographic lexicon.

For example, prefixes are encoded as un_ and re_, with underscore lines indicating that letter strings can only attach to their right, while suffixes are encoded as _ity and _er, with underscore lines indicating that letter strings can only be placed to their left.
This positional information encoding scheme strictly requires [1] affixes to only be in one position within a letter string and [2] such a position needs to always be at the edges of letter strings.
